speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE PRIME MINISTER-REFERENCE TO VOTE ON FIRST READING OF BILL, MAY 12
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that yesterday a bill was introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). When Mr. Speaker proceeded to read it a first time objection was taken. A vote followed, and it was decided that the bill should be read a first time. In my view that was all to the good. I notice however that some of the press are misinterpreting the nature of the vote. I have before me, for example, one newspaper which says: "PM"-I presume that refers to myself

"votes for no secrecy in income tax." I did not do anything of the kind. I voted for the first reading of a bill, to which I think an hon. member is entitled, unless there is something particularly obnoxious to the house in his bill. I cannot imagine anything that would help to do more to destroy the hon. member's bill than to have it read so that the house might know what it contains.
I wish to have it clearly understood that my vote was given simply on the basis of the right of a member to have his bill read the first time. The decision as to the principle would come up on the motion for second reading. However that motion has not yet been made -and I doubt if it will be made at any time this session. What I have said as to my vote applies I think equally as to the votes of many others given at the time.

Mr. Speaker, on April 20, when there was a celebration in honour of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), I suggested we should celebrate the birthdays of all members of parliament. Today is the birthday of one of our colleagues who, although he does not belong to my party, is the only privy councillor left in the House of Commons from the Bennett regime. He is a most likeable man,
and he has achieved the rare distinction of being the only person who has spiritual authority over the chief opposition whip, his son-in-law. I refer of course to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe (Mr. Rowe). This does not mean that I subscribe to all the policies the hon. member advocates; but I do congratulate him, offer him my best wishes, and express the hope that on the next occasion of a birthday anniversary one of our colleagues will offer the good wishes of the whole House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) in extending warm congratulations to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simeoe. The hon. member, in point of service in the house, is one of the oldest members. He has taken a most faithful and prominent part in the discharge of his duties here as well as having been a long time in public life. Those of us who have associated with him in parliament over the years will be the first to wish him continued health, strength and happiness for many years to come. This wish I am sure will be shared by all hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, while this is somewhat unusual, nevertheless it is appreciated. I should like particularly to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), both of whom have served many years in the house. It is a source of great pleasure to me to have been associated with them, and I can assure them I have always had the most kindly personal feelings toward them. May I reciprocate by offering them my good wishes and expressing the hope that they may celebrate many more birthdays-and that in that event many more of us may be here on this side to congratulate them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Resolved', that a sum not exceeding $'89,567,384.33, being one-twelfth of the amount of each of the several items to be voted, as set forth in the main estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1949, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament, and in addition thereto the sum of $17,982,745.67. being one-sixth of the amount of items 43. 151. 154, 155, 447, 541 and 542 of the said estimates be granted to His Majesty on account for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1949.
I thought the Minister of Finance would make a brief statement with respect to this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the proposed resolution, provision is being made for an additional one-twelfth of the main estimates, and an additional one-sixth of certain special items which provide for services coming up for payment within the early part of this year. These additional items are item 43 in the agriculture estimates covering freight assistance on western feed grains; items 151, 154 and 155, which relate to the Senate and the
Interim Supply

House of Commons, where, as hon. members will appreciate, the greater part of the expense has to be met early in the year; item 447 of the estimates of trade and commerce, which cover exhibitions, and where an additional amount is required at an early day for the expenses of the international trade fair which is being held in Toronto from May 31 to June 12; items 541 and 542, for estimated additional requirements in the Department of Veterans Affairs to cover increases in pensions and war veterans allowances which have either been adopted by the *house or are now under consideration.
The form of the bill which will be founded upon this resolution is exactly the same as the bill which has been presented in previous years. Of course the passage of the bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of hon. members to discuss any item in the estimates which will come up for consideration from time to time during the remainder of the session. I give the usual undertaking that such rights and privileges will be respected and not curtailed and restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure.

Mr. Chairman, the matter before us is spoken of as interim supply. Interim supply means the granting of huge sums of money to the government for its purposes, practically without debate. The minister is now asking that one-twelfth of the total amount of this year's estimates be voted without debate. Prior to this one-sixth of the total amount was passed under a similar motion. When this measure passes one-quarter of the total supply will have been voted, without debate. The reason why this motion comes before us is that we are now in the early part of a new financial year and the government has financial obligations, salaries to pay and other expenses to meet. The government finds itself without money and has to ask for a measure of this kind, to be passed practically without debate.
There is no question that the house will grant requests of this kind when they are made under similar circumstances. I rose simply to say that this practice, which is not a wise one, arises from the fact that the budget is not brought down early enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has nothing to do with the budget.

That is the moral of my remarks. An opportunity is not given, to deal with all these matters and to pass the budget, and so we are asked for these interim amounts. As I said, one-sixth has been voted already, and

another one-twelfth is being asked for, making one-quarter of the whole. The only point I wish to make is that the budget, including the estimates, should be considered earlier in the session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the remarks of my hon. friend call for a brief comment. Obviously, of course, the date on which the budget is brought down has nothing to do with the date on which supply is voted. The budget simply outlines the means by which the taxes will be raised to provide for the expenses of government, and that is a completely separate function from the voting of supply by the committee of supply.
There is nothing new in voting interim supply, as my hon. friend has indicated; but each year when it is asked for I listen to a repetition of this statement, that it is improper to vote large sums like this without debate. I w7ant to point out to the country what is well known, of course, to the house, that the estimates, which indicate the sums of money which parliament will be asked to provide for the public service of the financial year, are prepared early in the year. They were tabled this year in good time-in the month of February, I think-and have been before hon. members ever since that time. They are discussed, it is true, and formally voted in committee of supply; but my experience has been that the discussion in committee of supply rarely relates to the item under discussion and never suggests that an item be reduced. I have been here some little time and I recall no case in which the opposition has suggested that an item of proposed expenditure be reduced. The house and the country have been aware for months of the government's estimates of the amounts required to maintain the services of the country for the year. The practice of voting interim supply-one-sixth or one-twelfth of the estimates, as the case may be-is not for the purposes of the government as a government, but to carry on the essential services of the country.
I am not taking exception to what my hon. friend has said, but the date on which the budget is brought down has nothing whatever to do with the date on which the house may or may not be able to discuss the items of supply. Let me add that consideration of the estimates by the committee of supply has been unavoidably but inevitably delayed by the necessity of considering other measures such as emergency exchange conservation and the like. I must, however, take exception to any suggestion that the government has delayed the consideration of supply by not bringing down the budget.

Ways and Means-Interim Supply

Mr. Chairman, this is the eighty-third day of the session and we have had little or no opportunity yet of discussing the main estimates. While it is true that the minister must have money to run the sendees of the country, I would point out that businessmen and retail merchants and others have been looking for retrenchment in government expenditures. Practically all we are doing now in committee of supply is holding a post mortem after the money is spent. That is no way to conduct the business of the country. The government is spending money like water. I can see no sign of retrenchment in the main estimates or the supplementaries. We are being asked to vote large sums of money for bonuses, subventions and subsidies for the prairie provinces, and the other provinces do not get anything. There are manjr items here for interim supply, one for 880,000,000, another for $17,000,000, and so on. These expenditures, under this method of conducting the business of the country, really mean expenditures and taxation without representation. The house is abdicating its functions to the executive. It is a dangerous principle. The expenditures for civil government in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier amounted in 1897 to $36,000,000. and the population of the country has increased by only one-third or one-quarter since; but the civil estimates now are nearly two billions.
There should be some better way of conducting public business. The municipalities would be bankrupt if they did business'in this way. The auditor general should have wider powers to deal with some of these expenditures. The Minister of Finance may take this humorously, but it is no laughing matter for the working classes I represent. Government extravagance and lack of retrenchment, added to the high cost of living, are becoming scandalous, and the public will not stand for it. We should have some redress of grievances before we are asked to vote any further interim supply on this eighty-third day of the session.
I do not rise to object to passing interim supply but rather to take exception to the minister's statement that nobody has ever moved to reduce an item of supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said that I had never heard it done.

The minister was
sitting in the house in the session of 1946 when we were discussing the administration of the Department of Veterans Affairs and my colleague the hon. member for Lake Centre moved that a certain item be reduced to one dollar. Despite the fact that the minister never explained what the item was for, the government supporters trooped in and we were voted down.

speechtext: Did not my hon. friend suggest that the agriculture estimates ought to be $80,000,000 instead of $40,000,000?

Certainly I did, and I gave reasons why.

speechtext: Resolved, that a sum not exceeding $89,567,384.33, being one-twelfth of the amount of each of the several items to be voted, as set forth in the main estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1949, laid before the House of Commons at the present session of parliament, and in addition thereto the sum of $17,982,745.67, being one-sixth of the amount of items 43, 151, 154, 155, 447, 541 and 542 of the said estimates be granted to His Majesty on account for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1949.

I do not want the minister to say that the question I am about to raise is one which should be dealt with by the rules committee, of which I am a member; so I anticipate and protect myself beforehand. Has the government given serious consideration this session or in previous sessions to the whole question of dealing with the estimates of the various departments in a much more efficient way? Time after time, in session after session, members on both sides of the house have contended that our system of dealing with the estimates would not commend itself to any business handling even a fraction of the amount that this house is asked to vote from year to year. This is a matter that rests with the government rather than with other parties or with private members, because it would have to be a matter of government policy before any other system could be brought before the rules committee or before parliament.
The estimates of the Department of External Affairs are the only ones, outside of the railway estimates, that are dealt with in

detail by committees before they are dealt with by the house. If the minister has carefully scrutinized the work of these committees he must have found that they have done a reasonably good job in investigating the details of the expenditures of money by the departments concerned.
Suggestions have been made from time to time. One was that the various committees of the house might have referred to them at each session the estimates of the department whose activities are closely related to the kind of work that they are supposed to do. On the other hand, it has been suggested that a committee on estimates ought to be set up in the house which would deal with the question of estimates generally. That would be different from the public accounts committee, which, as I understand it, considers the auditor general's report. On every ground it would be distinctly different from the ordinary committees. I am not here to advocate one scheme or plan as against another, but I do advocate a change in a system which must have worked all right when we had a few million dollars to vote year after year but is not satisfactory now. We have the same machinery and we are doing the same thing in parliament that we did when I first came here twelve years ago-and twelve years is a short time compared with the length of time that some other hon. members on both sides of the house have been here. We are spending at least five times as much as we did when I first came here, and passing appropriations of five times as much money as we did at that time. Surely the situation calls for some reform.
The minister and the government might give serious consideration to this matter, because I think they will find on all sides a strong feeling of approval, of some change. People who are in business, people who are used to handling large sums of money and seeing that it is properly spent, must find this kind of arrangement antiquated, to say the least, and certainly not always productive of the best kind of audit and examination of our public expenditures. I ask the minister if he will consider the suggestion. Having brought it to his attention I think I have at least discharged part of my duty in connection with a serious matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peel has raised an interesting and important question, one to which, speaking for myself, I have given a good deal of consideration. It is not easy, though, to find what would be an acceptable alternative method of dealing with estimates. I am told that in the British parliament they do not give the detailed consideration to estimates that we do in our house; that

the estimates of the service departments are always considered in some detail, and several days are set aside for that purpose, but that the estimates of almost every department are simply passed en bloc. No opportunity is given for detailed consideration. Each year certain departments are selected and the estimates are discussed in some detail. That is one method. As hon. members will appreciate, it is not always the estimate which provides for the largest amount that provokes the greatest discussion. An estimate of an expenditure of 810,000 or 815,000 may promote more discussion and arouse more interest among members than one which involves $50,000,000 or $60,000,000. Therefore one cannot take the size of the estimate as a test of the amount of time that should be given to its discussion. The impression I have got from members is that in respect to various departments- fisheries, agriculture, trade and commerce, or whatever it may be-where special interest lies, they feel that they want an opportunity in the house to discuss these estimates and get information from the minister. I have not been given the impression that members would be satisfied to have these estimates considered and passed by a small committee.
Opportunity for discussion in the house is still guaranteed to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and I do not think it would save much time to refer them to a committee. I simply mention that to point out some of the difficulties with which I know all hon. members are familiar. All I can say is that I have not yet been able to think of a solution which would be generally acceptable. Perhaps that inspiration may come to me later.

The minister has referred-no doubt correctly -to the substantial difference in practice which prevails in the British house. Has he fully considered what I understand to be the very different procedure which they adopt before the estimates are finally brought down to the house? I think he will agree it is different, and perhaps he knows more about the actual difference than I do. I suggest that is well worthy of consideration from our point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not greatly different. Of course these estimates receive long, detailed and painstaking consideration by treasury board. May I say that my opening gambit to each member who came into treasury board with these estimates was: "The only savings that will be made in expenditures this year will

Ways and Means-Interim Supply
be made in this room". I was referring to my office in the east block, where we were holding the meeting. I said: "There will not be any savings made when these estimates are being considered by the house, because in my experience that is not the place where reductions of expenditures are made. Any savings on public expenditures will be made right inside this room." I simply mention this to show that that is where the estimates of expenditures receive detailed and painstaking consideration. I may be mistaken, but so far as I am aware our method does not differ substantially from that under which estimates of expenditures are prepared in Great Britain. The estimates are prepared by the departments. They are submitted to the treasury, and then are settled by the treasury, and by the government finally, before being presented to parliament. That is the procedure which is followed here.

That has not yet been

done, and I hope that further consideration will be given to the matter by the financial authorities.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not propose to discuss the other matter which is before the house, and which is on the order paper, with respect to the establishment and increases.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We are all in favour of that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Without going into that question, leaving it aside at the moment, I would point out that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is somewhat in error about the staff that does not come under the civil service commission, and their increases. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does the hon. member know when it was done, or can he find out?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: First the messengers got theirs.

speechtext: All messengers, or just the confidential messengers?

You have been busy with the voters' list, anyway.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am quite sure they got their increases.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I hope you are right.

I do not wish to assume any credit for what the government tries to do for the staff of the House of Commons, but the government should be congratulated on having taken the matter into serious consideration and having submitted to us a list of the proposed increases. They are not complete; they are supposed to be completed and adjusted. I wish however to pay a special tribute to the two members representing Ottawa for the care they are taking not only of the employees of the House of Commons but of the whole staff in the civil service in the city of Ottawa. I refer especially to the hon. member for Ottawa West, the very able assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and Trade and Commerce.
I have been dealing with the hon. member for many years and I have always admired his patience and his devotion to his electors.

Ways and Means-Interim Supply
No one knows what it is to be a member representing the city of Ottawa, with long lines of people waiting to be heard, having a good word for each of them, and ready to help anyone. That is what has been done by the two members representing the city of Ottawa, especially by the hon. member for Ottawa West. I bow to the hon. member and assure him of my sincere admiration for his understanding of the problems of civil servants. The hon. member deserves every praise; and he should have some other reward than that of being parliamentary assistant to a cabinet minister. I do not know how on earth a member of parliament can represent one of the constituencies in the city of Ottawa and at the same time fulfil his duties as parliamentary assistant to a cabinet minister. It is bej'ond me. I cannot understand it.
For a time I had my office near that of a former member, who is now Mr. Justice Chevrier. At that time he represented one of the Ottawa ridings. He could not go out of his office without meeting forty or fifty people who were waiting for him, and when those forty or fifty had gone they were replaced by another forty or fifty. He never complained about it; he was always pleasant to all.
Is it not admirable? I have the greatest admiration for the hon. gentleman and I take this opportunity to say so. I say it with the utmost pleasure. I consider it is my duty to say it, because at times I have business to do with the hon. member for Ottawa West. I have to call at his office.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Doesn't that apply to all hon. members from this area?

I have shown today that I appreciate the work of my colleagues, and I am proud to be one of theirs. On the other hand, outside of the hon. gentleman I have mentioned, there is no one of us who is at the same time a member for one of the Ottawa constituencies and parliamentary assistant to a cabinet minister w'ho is responsible for a department which has so much to do with everything. Therefore I am not minimizing the work of my other colleagues, for whom I have respect and admiration, when I say that the position of the hon. member for Ottawa West is unique and he deserves all our admiration.

I wish to add a word or two to the remarks made by the hon. member for Peel. I feel, as do a great many others-and I refer not only to members of this house but to the public in general-that sufficient time is not given to the consideration of the estimates. If we could spread out consideration of the various items, it would do much to foster greater confidence in our democratic system of government. We rush through, in the short time of just a few minutes, estimates dealing with hundreds of millions of dollars. If I sit down and no one else speaks, it will mean that we shall have passed this huge amount in a matter of ten minutes. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Peel is worthy of serious thought. Of course he is not the only one who in the past has made that suggestion. I think the government would be well advised to consider a method by which greater consideration could be given to the estimates.
That was not my purpose in rising, however, Mr. Chairman; it was rather to deal particularly with item 154. which covers the sessional stenographers. We shall be appointing, I believe, an additional number of permanent members to the stenographic staff; and they will be receiving employment the year around, with a stated yearly salary. I have no objection to the additional number who will be appointed or to any salary which might be set for their employment. But I do say that the sessional stenographers are not receiving sufficient pay; and I say that from a business standpoint. They are brought to Ottawa and are kept here for a period of six months. They pay their own transportation to and from Ottawa. They are paid at the rate of $5 a day. A	few	years	ago	theystarted out at $4, and	they	were	given an
increase; after a certain period of employment they were given SI extra, thus bringing the pay up to $5. So far as I know, that is the rate at which they are paid today.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit an interjection?
Yes.	.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I wholly	agree	with	him
that the pay should be higher. But just in order to have the record straight, may I say that the amount is now $5.90 a day. I agree with the hon. member that it should be higher, in view of the fact- that it is not year-round employment.

Yes, that is quite true. The point I am making is that they are only part-time employees.

Ways and Means-Interim Supply

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is right.

I think it is recognized today by practically every employer of labour that a part-time man is entitled to a higher rate than that which is paid to a permanent employee. For that reason, although I do not wish to press the matter, I thought it was an opportune time to bring it to the attention of the Minister of Finance or the Speaker, or the Clerk of the House-whoever happens to have jurisdiction as to that particular item1-so that consideration could be given to increasing the pay of the sessional stenographers. I have that particular class of employees in mind when I make these remarks. I go further: I think there should be an allowance for travelling expenses. If it is necessary to bring to Ottawa stenographers of this particularly efficient type, I believe they should be provided with transportation to and from their place of employment.

When this bill was brought down, my conception of the matter was that it was for the purpose of getting interim, supply, and that it did not open up a detailed discussion of the estimates. The purpose for which the money is required is clearly set out in the bill: agriculture, freight assistance on western grains-and I think most hon. members will agree that it is necessary-and so forth. I am not disagreeing with anything that is in the bill. It simply represents a certain amount of the regular estimates necessary now in order to enable the departments to carry on. It is unfortunate that the discussion of the House of Commons staff was injected into the discussion at this time, because-

I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman.. I referred particularly to one of the items which was included in this bill, namely, item 154. If any objection is taken it would not be to the part of the staff of the House of Commons to which I referred, but rather to the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I was not specifying anybody. I merely said it was unfortunate that it was injected into the discussion-
No matter where it came from.

[DOT]-for the simple reason there is already on the order paper a motion by the Secretary of State which will enable anyone to carry on a detailed discussion of that particular question. Now that the matter has been injected, I have just this to say- and I think the chairman himself can accept responsibility for allowing this discussion to

take place. On the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and what he said was concurred in by the senior member for Halifax, I say that the question of the stenographic staff is one that cannot be passed over by just saying that the salaries are too high or too low. It is a question that requires detailed study. It is a matter concerning 155 people who are in this building for the purpose of rendering certain services to members of parliament, and that aspect of it must be considered. I think the most important question in connection with the sessional stenographers is the matter of transportation. They come from long distances, and they are not employed the year round. I think they should be provided with transportation.
The hon. member agrees with me on that point.
Yes. I say it is a point that should be considered. Second, and I think more important than fixing a higher rate, is the question of superannuation.
That is right,
A great many of the girls who are sessional stenographers have been on the staff for twenty or twenty-five years.
Permanent temporaries.

They have reached the age where they should be retiring. Adequate retirement provision should be made for them. If you continue as you are, what you are making of the stenographic pool is not a pool that will give service to the members of the house, but rather a home in which to take care of people whom you are afraid to put out because the system has not provided for them.
I am not going to enter upon a detailed discussion of the matter now, because I said it was unfortunate that the question had been opened up under this bill. But when the Secretary of State brings in the motion he now' has on the order paper with regard to establishment and revisions in classifications, I am going to say something about it and make certain definite recommendations.
With this short explanation I hope this bill will pass to enable the departments to get along.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I suppose, strictly speaking, it is in order when this bill is before the committee to discuss any item which may be in the main estimates. It has been the practice when the minister has moved for interim

Ways and Means-Interim Supply
supply to make general observations and perhaps to refer to particular grievances, but I do not think it has been customary to discuss items in detail.
I should imagine a good many members might wish to speak about the matter of the House of Commons staff. If we were to proceed to do that now, this would develop into a full-dress debate. I appeal to members of the committee to defer discussion of that question until the motion standing in the name of the Secretary of State is before the house.
I wish to point out that the question of the salaries of the house staff is not within the jurisdiction of treasury board or of the Minister of Finance. It is a question which is in the control of the house itself, and which will no doubt be discussed when the resolution is before the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On that last point, it seems to me we should not for ever be pushed back and forth from one authority to the other. I do feel it is not fair for the Minister of Finance to put the responsibility for this solely upon t he officials of the house. They may have their ideas, but they cannot-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not the officials of the house; it is the house itself. The house is master of its own staff. The staff of the House of Commons is not subject to treasury board control, as are the staffs of every other department of government. That is the point I wish to make clear. Treasury board, of which I am chairman, and which is a committee of cabinet ministers, does exercise general financial supervision over expenditures and has control over the regular departments of government. But the House of Commons, and rightly so, has always been very jealous of its prerogatives and its control over its own staff. The committee of the house which considers these matters of establishment and the like is the internal economy commission, consisting of four cabinet ministers, of which I am one, and Mr. Speaker. It is a committee of the house, not a committee of the government; and Mr. Speaker is chairman. The estimates of expenditures of the house are presented by Mr. Speaker. The Clerk of the House in that respect occupies the same position as a deputy minister in a government department.
I have interjected this by way of explanation, because I think there is some misconception as to the government's responsibility for salaries and the like in the House of Commons. It is not the government's responsibility at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister says this matter comes within the purview and responsibility of the House of Commons itself, not of the government. Does that mean that members of the House of Commons can propose salary increases or salary changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, I would assume so. I am not an expert on the rules, but I assume that is so.
Where would a private member of the house get with a motion to increase these salaries?
Not very far.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps not very far; but that is-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a different matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: We would be told that it involved increased expenditure and we would have to get approval either of the internal economy commission or of the treasury board itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think that is correct; that is completely incorrect. I take exception to that, and I think the Clerk of the House would sustain me in it. A member of the house who proposed a resolution for expenditures with respect to service of the house would not have to get permission from treasury board or from the government. He would not have to get permission of the internal economy commission. I may be wrong but I notice the Clerk is nodding his head, and I think I am right.
Would the Speaker of the house not have to go before the Minister of Finance with his estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Because it is in the minister's office that they are made. Suppose they are too high; would it not be up to the minister to cut them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no power to cut them.
But you would, though.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not.
You would have no power, but you would do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no power to cut them. All I am interested in is in putting this responsibility where it lies.
Passing the buck.

With respect to this item of 87,750,000 on freight assistance, will the minister make a statement as to what has

Ways and Means-Interim Supply
been used already out of this fund, and the quality of feed grains now in storage in the west and on the western farms which he expects to ship in using up this $7,750,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give that information. As I said a minute ago, in passing interim supply the minister does not give that kind of information about expenditures. If he were to do so he would have to have with him the details of all the items. The invariable practice in interim supply, so far as my experience goes, is that we do not give details and members do not expect to receive detailed information on the items. That is all asked for when the main estimates are being considered. I shall be glad, therefore, to give the information when this item is reached in the main estimates. Or if my hon. friend wishes to have the information in the meantime. Of course I shall gladly get it for him. But if we were to attempt today to go into the details of all these matters-
The Minister of Agriculture is in his seat. Perhaps he would give us a brief statement as to how he expects to use the $7,750,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is an amount of $20,000,000 for the whole year. What is asked for here is to cover until July 31. It has already been announced that in the supplementary estimates provision will be made for the continuance of this form of assistance during the coming crop year. I cannot give further information now because I have not the details here.
The Minister of Agriculture is here, and he knows what was used last year.
The Minister of Agriculture gave that information when his own estimates were under consideration the other night. It is on Hansard.
For the coming year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The explanation I have on that is this. The main estimates of course include provision only to the end of the present year, July 31. This will have the effect of concentrating the bulk of claims coming for payment into the -first quarter of the fiscal year. Those in April, May, June and July will require a substantial proportion of the vote at this time. That is what my officials, who watch the rate at which these moneys have to be paid out, inform me. In effect we are asking for what it is estimated will be required before the end of June to cover these items.

Mr. Chairman, since a matter having to do with employees of the House of Commons has been brought up, I wish to ask one question about it. The minister says this matter comes within the jurisdiction of the house as distinguished from the government itself. He has indicated that the body which represents the house in dealing with matters of this kind is the internal economy commission, of which he has told us he is a member. Reference has been made to certain reports tabled the other day, and a resolution on the order paper with respect to these officials. Certain salary increases have been proposed, and I have heard no opposition to those increases. There is in the minds of many members of the House of Commons the thought that some of the employees of the house have not had an increase within the last year. My question is this: Is it correct that certain employees of the House of Commons have not had an increase within the last year? If so, is it the intention of the internal economy commission or the government-and I fail to see much difference between the two, since that commission is made up of a number of government officials-to see that all employees, or those at least who have not had one, receive an increase this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a question which, in the organization of the House of Commons, could more properly be put to Mr. Speaker. I cannot vouch for it, because it is not my department and not my responsibility, but I am informed that there is no employee. of the House of Commons who has not had an increase within approximately the last eighteen months or two years.

I suggest then, that the internal economy commission order an examination of these positions, because I am informed that increases have not been made to all these employees within the last year. I am informed also that the increases made to some within the last two years covered only the cost of living bonus. I ask that those who may not have received favourable consideration during the last twelve months be given that consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no doubt that Mr. Speaker will have taken note of my hon. friend's observations.

There is one other thing, if I may be permitted to bring it up at this time. There is a resolution before us with

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR AND ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR

speechtext:
Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 282, to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the other day when I asked to have the resolution advanced it was suggested to me that I should make a statement having to do with the level of the water in Long lake and with the dam which is being considered for the South Saskatchewan river. I would suggest that neither one of these matters is dealt with in the bill now before us, because the bill simply provides for the appointment of certain officials. However, I am quite willing to make a statement with regard to both these projects. If hon. members desire to ask questions at the time the statement is being made it might be better for us to go into committee although I am prepared to make the statement on second reading.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR AND ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR
speechtext: Go ahead and make the statement.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR AND ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR
speechtext:
As I suggested the other day, the bill contains only one section which provides:
The minister may appoint a director of rehabilitation and an associate director of rehabilitation, and such temporary technical and other officers and employees as he may deem necessary and expedient for carrying out the provisions of this act and the salaries and expenses of all persons appointed under this section shall be fixed by the governor in council.
That section, with the exception of the first two lines and the phrase, "persons appointed under this section" in the latter part of the section, is as it was in the original act. In other words, under the original act the mini-ter has the authority to appoint such temporary technical and other officers and employees as he may deem neceessary and expedient for carrying out the provisions of this act, and the salaries and expenses of all shall be fixed by the governor in council.
The reason for bringing this amendment before the house is that we desired to appoint as director of rehabilitation a gentleman who is a member of the civil service in the Department of Agriculture. Being a permanent appointee, he is entitled to certain superannuation rights which he has established over a long period of service. When this position was offered to him he said that he desired to maintain his present position in relation to superannuation. After considerable discussion and an examination into the means of bringing this about, this amendment was decided upon as being the reasonable way to do it. The minister would simply be given authority to appoint a person who would be permanent, that is, a person who is already a permanent member of the civil service.
It was decided at the same time that an associate director of rehabilitation should be appointed. This is necessary, partly because additional responsibilities have been added to the prairie farm rehabilitation organization through the estimates which were passed last year and which are before the house this session. Larger projects, such as the South Saskatchewan project and other activities, will be carried on, not only in the Palliser triangle but in other parts of Canada. It was felt that we should have here in the Department of Agriculture an official who would be in direct touch at all times with the director in Regina.
I was asked the other night who the individual would be. That has not been decided, but it is anticipated that he will be either a member of the civil service or someone who could qualify as a civil servant through service in some other office. Since the individual has not yet been selected, I am not able to give his name to the house. It is anticipated that when the appointment is made the person will be either in the same position as the director in relation to superannuation or be able to qualify to be placed in that position. If that is the case, then the appointment would be made under this amendment; but if that is

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
not the case and if we go outside those who can qualify for the civil service to find someone, then he could be appointed under the terms of the act as it stood before this amendment is made. I think that is sufficient to explain the position in relation to the bill itself.
Since I stated the other evening that I would discuss the two other matters in question, I think I should do so at this time. The first has to do with the water levels in Long lake. As was stated by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) this is the largest body of water in the settled portion of Saskatchewan. The lake is about seventy miles long and from five to six miles wide at its widest parts. It stores a very considerable amount of water.
The lake is peculiarly situated, in that water runs into it from the Qu'Appelle river which is located about a mile or a mile and a half from the south end of the lake. Originally there was a natural stream which flowed from the Qu'Appelle river into the south end of Long lake. During the time of high water in the spring the water would run into the lake, but if the lake filled up above its natural level the water would flow out from the lake during the remaining part of the season until the level was brought down to the bottom of the old creek.
Some years ago a channel was constructed from the south end of the lake to the Qu'Appelle, and at the same time a dam was put in the Qu'Appelle river. That was done many years ago when the natural resources of the west were under the control of the federal government and before the province of Saskatchewan was formed. The dam which was put in the river at the south end of the lake was put there for the purpose of raising the level of Long lake in order that a boat could be operated on Long lake, and at that period a boat was operated on that lake, going north from Valeport. I have seen the boat often myself in the earlier days.
'As a result of putting the dam in the river and raising the water level of the lake, the parties who owned the flats at the south end of the lake took action against the federal government for having flooded their land, and my memory is that they secured damages in the amount of $50,000. From that time on, these lands were often flooded. They are natural hay lands, but they were flooded sometimes during a greater part of the season. That continued down until the drought period began in the latter part of the 1920's and the early 1930's. During that period I happened to be in the government of Saskatchewan, and a

damage suit was started against the federal government, because at that time the resources were still under its control, on account of the way in which the dam was being operated by Ottawa. In other words, it was maintained that in order to keep Long lake at a higher level than it otherwise would have been the dam was closed and the water was run into Long lake, and in the summer when hay should be growing on the flats below the dam the water was allowed to flood the flats, which, instead of growing hay, were growing what we called foxtail. So the owners down the valley started an action. About that time the operation of the dam was transferred from the interior department at Ottawa to the department of highways of Saskatchewan, to be operated in such a manner as to provide that the waters did not flood these lands at the WTong time. As a result of the transfer of the operation of the dam, the suit was not proceeded with.
A little later, 1931 to be exact, the natural resources were transferred to the province, and from that time on until P.F.R.A. took an interest in the levels of the lake the dam was operated by the department of highways of Saskatchewan. I think it is now operated under an arrangement between the department of highways at Regina and P.F.R.A., but latterly under the direction largely of P.F.R.A.
This spring, when word was coming through that there were considerable floods in western Canada as a result of the rapid thawing of snow toward the end of April, I wired the office at Regina, or had Mr. Stevenson wire the director of P.F.R.A. at Regina, as follows: Director P.F.R.A.
MeCallum Hill Bldg.
Regina, Sask.
Minister wishes assurance Craven dam being operated to divert flood waters to Long Lake. Please let us have brief report !by wire.
A. L. Stevenson.
Later that same day, April 28, we received this wire:
Moose Jaw, Sask.
April 28, 1948
A. L. Stevenson,
Office of Deputy Minister Department of Agriculture,
Ottawa.
Re telegram Craven dam being operated to divert all possible water to Long lake and we have purposely broken our Valeport dyke to permit free flo,w. Over four thousand acre feet entering daily and lake has already risen two and one-half feet over last year.
E. L. Gray,
Superintendent Water Development P.FRA..
After the discussion which took place here the other day, I again had Mr. Stevenson

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act .
wire the director of P.F.R.A. at Regina, under date of May 11, as follows:
Director, P.F.R.A.
910 McCallum Hill Building,
Regina, Saskatchewan
Please let us have a report for use of minister further to your wire of April twenty-eighth regarding level of Long lake. Advise if diversion continuing.
A. L. Stevenson.
We received this wire in reply, dated May 11:
A. L. Stevenson,
10 Confederation Bldg., Ottawa, Ontario
Re telegram diversion Long lake continuing at full capacity of C.P.R. structure at Valeport. Holding water very high in Craven Lumsden area to get full flow. Long lake rising steadily. Will give definite measurement during week.
E. L. Gray,
Superintendent of Water Development.
I then telephoned the office in Regina and said that definite measurement during the week would not be much help to us this afternoon in the house when we were discussing this matter, and that I had given the house an undertaking that I would give as definite information as possible before the bill was passed. As a result of that telephone conversation, I have this information:
Mr. Gray informs me that up to last night the water in Long lake had been raised over four feet above the level existing at the end of last season. The diversion is continuing and the water in the lake is being raised at the Tate of about one inch per day. It is expected that a further increase of at least one foot, andi possibly more, can be achieved. This means a net increase of at least five feet altogether.
When one remembers that Long lake is seventy miles long and five or six miles wide at some points one can understand that a very considerable amount of water ran into the lake this year in order to fill it up to that level. I would say, however, that not all the water came into the lake out of the Qu'Appelle river, because other streams all around run into the lake and these streams have, of course, been adding to the volume of water in the lake, but they at all times add all their water to that lake. The only place where we can control diversion into the lake is on the Qu'Appelle river, and I am sure it will be realized from what has been said that everything which could be done to raise the level of Long lake as a result of the operation of the dam has been done this year, and the result obtained is, I think, very satisfactory.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR AND ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR
speechtext: Can the minister say how much below the high level that still leaves the lake?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTOR AND ASSOCIATE DIRECTOR
speechtext:
Unfortunately I am not able to do that, but I wruld think it is getting back very close to what was the normal level; probably not up to what was the high level. At one time the level was down eight feet, and it may have been down ten feet at one time. But the level was increased somewhat last season, and five feet of water has been added again this year.
The other question raised1 had to do with expenditures on the South Saskatchewan. At the present time one is quite within the rules to discuss expenditures on the South Saskatchewan under the P.F.R.A. vote or in connection with legislation having to do with P.F.R.A. But so far as regards the future development of the South Saskatchewan, the building of the South Saskatchewan dam and everything that would go along with it, such works would not be carried on under votes for P.F.R.A.
The reason I say that the votes up to date would be votes which could quite properly be discussed under P.F.R.A. is that one of the functions of P.F.R.A. is to investigate all the possibilities within the P.F.R.A. area; that is, within the old Palliser triangle, and to report from time to time as to what those possibilities are. But the total amount which is voted for P.F.R.A. has never been more than $3,000,000 for what we generally call P.F.R.A. work. I think in one or two sessions $3,500,000 was voted, but $500,000 of it was for special work being carried on to demonstrate whether water could be pumped out of the Saskatchewan river and brought down to within eighteen miles of the city of Moose Jaw and stored in the sands there and utilized for city purposes later on. But this house has provided for expenditures under the act as originally drawn, and as it is still drawn, of about $3,000,000.
One of the investigational operations that has been carried on is to determine just what could be done with the waters of the South Saskatchewan river. We have been carrying on engineering investigations, beginning, so far as Saskatchewan is concerned, up on the Alberta boundary line. As a matter of fact, we carried on investigations farther west than that, but the investigations that we are concerned about in so far as the bridge north of Swift Current is concerned, and so far as the dam farther down the Saskatchewan river is concerned, started at the Alberta boundary line, and we have investigated two or three different possibilities. One is the matter of pumping water out of the Saskatchewan river at different points and irrigating table land areas similar to that which has been irrigated

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
just west of Medicine Hat, where a very-considerable area is irrigated by the pumping of water up a hundred feet or so and then distributing it over a table land, which is only part way up toward the height of land at the top of the valley.
We did make examinations all along the Saskatchewan river in an effort to determine at how many points a similar type of irrigation could be carried on. While we were doing that, we made investigations by boring as to possible sites for a dam. As a result of these investigations we have located ten possible sites, and these are indicated on a map. I think we have spent about 8250,000 in boring holes and carrying on investigational work at these different sites. Eventually we came to the conclusion that there are only two places at which a dam could be built which could serve the purpose of most people who discuss the possibility of a dam there of any kind. One is near Outlook, which I think is numbered S, and the other is near the mouth of Coteau creek which is numbered 10 on the plan. No. 10 is the site which has been reported most favourably upon; but there is no engineer who, up to the present moment, will take the responsibility for saying that there is no possibility of making any mistake in building a dam at that site. Therefore the borings are still going on.
The report which was tabled in the house during the last session, and a copy of which I have before me, is noted as an interim report on the South Saskatchewan river development, It will be noted that it is not a final report; it is an interim report. This interim report shows that all the information which they have been able to gain up to the present would indicate that a dam could be built near the mouth of Coteau creek, and it would serve certain purposes. The information which the report contains is to the effect that if [DOT] borings demonstrate that the formations below are what they have reason now to believe they are, it will be possible to build a dam there very much of the same type of construction and with the same kind of materials as dams have been constructed on the Missouri river in the United States at two or three different points.
It is said that the dam ought to be about 210 feet high. From the bottom of the river basin as it now is to the top of the dam would be about 210 feet. It is said that if we built a dam that high we would still have to do some pumping in order to get water out for irrigation purposes in certain areas; but that a dam built that high would be 120 feet higher than the embankment along the river

which separates the South Saskatchewan river from the Qu'Appelle river valley. The distance from the South Saskatchewan to the Qu'Appelle is only a matter of some two miles. Therefore, if the dam were built 210 feet high the water level would be such that at least half of the water intended to be stored would go naturally down the Qu'Appelle and would not remain in the Saskatchewan at all. Not only must there be a dam built across the Saskatchewan river of a very considerable size and at great cost, but there would have to be a dam built along the east bank of the Saskatchewan river in order to prevent the waters going out, excepting under regulation, into the Qu'Appelle. It is said that if we were to build these structures the cost would be in the neighbourhood of $66,000,000. It is also said that the lake which would be created would be probably 145 miles long, and that it would be of varying widths, depending upon the widths of the Saskatchewan river valley. It would flood a very considerable area of land which is now being cultivated, and it would cause some persons to be moved from the valley up onto the higher lands. Further all the expenses in connection with this matter and the construction of the dam would total somewhere in the neighbourhood of $66,000,000.
As a result of building a dam of that kind, the water level just north of Swift Current where the ferry now is, at what is known as Saskatchewan Landing, would be raised to a level which would be some fifty-three feet above its present level. And it is at a point, at Saskatchewan Landing, where the ferry now is, that the Saskatchewan government desires to build a bridge. That bridge has been under discussion for many years. One has only to look at the area to see that the railways have been built up to the river or toward the river, from both the north side and the south side, but that no railway or traffic bridge has been built across the river at that point. The question that has been under discussion for some considerable time is as to whether the people who live on the two sides of the river should be asked to utilize the ferry until such time as the railway was prepared to join the provincial government at this point in doing what they have done at many other points in building a bridge across the river.
My understanding is that the people have become a little tired of waiting. They think the time has been too long already. They think a traffic bridge ought to be built. I understand that all groups who are discussing the matter are pretty well agreed that a traffic bridge ought to be built. The question that is under discussion out there at the

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
moment is, should it be built for an increased water level of fourteen feet or an increased -water level of fifty-three feet? The 14-foot level only became a matter of discussion when we were talking about another dam site. As I stated, there are ten of them. There was a time when we had a report which indicated that if we built a dam of a certain kind at a certain place the level would be raised fourteen feet. And it was on that assumption that plans were laid out for the building of a bridge which would provide for a water level fourteen feet higher than the present level.
I am sorry I am not in a position, and I do not think anyone is in a position, to state at this moment whether the large project which I have outlined in a few words, which would cost approximately 866,000,000, will be undertaken, and how soon it will be undertaken. The only thing I can state at the moment is that no project of that kind can be undertaken inside two years. It cannot be started inside two years. The reason is that all the best engineers we can employ tell us it has taken at least that long, in connection with all the large United States projects, to make the final decision, because of the borings that must be made. And they would not undertake to recommend to the government, until after two more seasons of investigational work had been carried on, whether that is the proper site at which to build a dam, and whether we should proceed on the basis that has been discussed up to the moment.
All I can say that is definite at the moment is that we are told by the engineers that it will take two years, this year and another, in order to examine fully into the possibility of constructing a dam at that location and keeping it there after it is built. The question as to whether they can make it stay or not does not depend on anything you can see at the surface. They have to bore some 200 feet at many points, extending back east and west from the river and in the basin of the river itself, in order to determine whether we can make the dam stay there.
So we have five or six outfits drilling holes and keeping records as to what the nature of the area is below where the dam is to be built, and as this dam would be a very considerable structure it will take some time. The shortest time in which it can be efficiently done-completed rather, because much of it has been done-would ;be this year and one more year.
What I wanted to point out was that until the end of that time these engineers are employed under the P.F.R.A. vote; but if at the end of that time the report is that this
is a proper site and that the dam might be built there, this government would consider proceeding with construction. After the federal government has so decided, we must then deal with three provincial governments. I have been dealing with them for the last year with regard to this structure and others, and in that time I have discovered some of the difficulties. I am going to give them to the house in order to indicate that we cannot speed these things up just as much as some of us would like to have them speeded up. Three provinces are concerned.
All these rivers we are discussing-the Red Deer, the Bow, the Saskatchewan, the Red, the Assiniboine, the Souris-are in the Nelson river 'basin. They all have their origin out-near the Rocky mountains or in them, in the province of Alberta, with the exception of the Souris, the Red and the Assiniboine. These rivers have their origin either in the province of Saskatchewan or down in the United States, but the larger streams all have their origin in the province of Alberta.
The province of Alberta is interested in retaining as much of the water as it is entitled to in the province, because I presume there are just as great acreages-I think I am right in saying there are just as great acreages-which could be irrigated in Alberta as there are in Saskatchewan, while there are lesser areas in Manitoba which might be benefited by irrigation. And so Alberta is interested in one thing, namely utilizing as much of the water as it is entitled to.
At the other extreme you have the province of Manitoba. They are interested in two or three things. The first is to see that lakes Manitoba and Winnipeg and other smaller lakes are kept at the proper level. They are as much interested in that as the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is in keeping up the level of Long lake, and therefore they must be consulted before we dam up any of these streams and make these large lakes we are talking about.
Not only that, but they say they are now reaching the point where the development of power is their main consideration, and the only place they can go, in order to develop additional power to what they now know of down in the south, is up north at the mouth of the Saskatchewan river. Therefore they are interested in what we do back along that river.
We have tried to have this matter settled by setting up a board. That board was proposed a year ago. We drew up an order in
3896

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
council here and presented it to the three provinces, suggesting that each of the provinces appoint its chief engineer, and we would appoint one from the P.F.R.A. and one from Mines and Resources. This board of five would divide these waters and say that we must allow a certain number of gallons to flow over the boundary of Alberta into Saskatchewan, and then allow a certain number of gallons to flow out of Saskatchewan into Manitoba.
We thought that board would be quite satisfactory, but we found that the provinces were not altogether agreeable. They thought the recommendations of the board ought to go back to the governments. We next attempted to have the provision of the veto apply, so as to allow a representative of one province to veto the decision.

We suggested that the decision ought to be unanimous, and that was acceptable to both Saskatchewan and Alberta but not to Manitoba. So ten days ago, when the premiers of the provinces were here, I had them together and they brought along with them some of their officials. We discussed the question again, and I think we finally agreed on a kind of board which will be satisfactory to all of us. The provision to be made is that this board can only recommend; it cannot decide anything.
In other words, the board will meet and figure out what they think the division of water ought to be among the three provinces, and an order in council will have to be passed by each of the provinces and by the federal government before we are in a position to proceed with any of these matters. I hope that it is not going to take too long, but I am not in a position to tell the house how long it will take. I think the engineers are in a position to say what amount of water has flowed from one province into another over a long period of time, and I hope that within a short time they will be able to recommend what they think ought to be allowed.

effect. After they are put into effect, of course each one of the projects will have to be again agreed upon, and we shall be required to demonstrate to the provinces concerned that we have so built these structures as to permit of the agreed upon proportion of the water passing from one province into another.
I need only to remind hon. members again that if we build this dam 210 feet high on the Saskatchewan-it is 120 feet above the level at which the waters go into the Qu'Appelle; the waters that go into the Qu'Appelle go into the Assiniboine; and the Assiniboine has been flooding the city of Brandon and the city of Portage during this season-that Manitoba is somewhat concerned about what we do.

I am sure the house has listened, Mr. Speaker, with interest to the minister's recital in connection with the projected dam on the Saskatchewan river. That is a matter of interest not only to the people of Saskatchewan but to the people throughout western Canada in general.
First I want to thank him for what he has told the house about what the P.F.R.A. department has done during the current year to maintain the level of Long lake, also known as Last Mountain lake. As he pointed out, this is the largest body of water in central Saskatchewan.
I now wish to refer to the Saskatchewan river project, the one to which he devoted a large portion of his remarks. That project has been a dream in the minds of the western farmers for a great many years. As far back as 1854 when Captain Palliser made his expedition which resulted in the finding of Kicking Horse pass, it was realized that there were areas of what are now Saskatchewan and Alberta which might never be utilized for farm purposes.
Only recently I was reading the diaries of Captain Palliser wherein he pointed out that a large area of what are now the western

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
provinces-from a point at Emerson in Manitoba, thence by a direct line to a point that is now Lloydminster; thence in a direct line to what is now Macleod-was an area so arid that he doubted whether it would ever be settled. The last survivor of the Palliser expedition, John Moberly of Prince Albert, who was water-boy with the expedition, some fifteen or eighteen years ago told me that as that expedition crossed the great western plains in 1854, they never believed that it would ever be settled. It was dry as a desert. However, it was settled. The history of that area has been that over periods of eight, nine and ten years, there has been good production followed by periods of similar length wherein drought has all but destroyed the hopes of the people living there; yet they have stayed on and continued to live there, hoping for a diminution in the length of these periods of drought or hoping that, with the passing of the years, the rainfall would not be as uncertain as in the past.
The project has been a dream. I know the interest shown by the minister. But as I listened to him, I could not but conclude that he was doubtful whether the building of a dam either at Outlook or at Coteau creek will be achieved within the immediate future. Indeed, on occasion when he has been speaking to western organizations, service clubs and the like, I have detected a higher degree of optimism as to this project than I did in his remarks today.

I do not think the minister, in what he said, holds out the hope that the people of western Canada expect. He has spoken at full length and most frankly. In spite of the arguments over water levels that are taking place regarding the bridge at Swift Current, the minds of the people in Saskatchewan are made up that this project must be undertaken.
Excuses for delay will not be accepted. As far back as 1943 Mr. George Spence, the former director, gave evidence before the reconstruction committee of the House of Commons. He was speaking with a vast experience behind him, and he said that $111 million should be spent on water development in the west. He outlined a plan which he thought was necessary to the development, not only of western Canada but of Canada as a whole.
This project may seem to be a great one' in so far as cost is concerned. Sixty-six million dollars is a large amount of money. However, if the plan is feasible it will mean dividends to the Canadian people. It will mean that large expenditures now being made today under P.F.A.A. will no longer be necessary. It will mean that areas which have been submarginal will become productive as have similar areas in the United States and in other parts of Canada where irrigation has been introduced. It will mean new hope to tens of thousands of people in the area which would be served by this dam. Fifty-three per cent of the population of Saskatchewan live within a radius of 125 miles of either of the suggested sites.
This is not a purely provincial matter. This matter is as national in scope as the building of canals in Ontario, Quebec or the maritimes. It is as national in scope as any project that can be brought before the Canadian parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I think we were all glad to hear the minister give his explanation this afternoon in regard to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and possible irrigation developments.
I am sure the members of this group will go along with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the demand he has made that something be done in the near future to irrigate those areas which it is feasible to irrigate.
As has been said before, the director of rehabilitation, Mr. L. B. Thomson, is an energetic and capable man. In my discussions with people in Saskatchewan who are trained in agricultural matters, I have always heard him spoken of most highly. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) are not able to be present this afternoon as they are attending committee meetings, but I know they are interested in what is to be done in connection with the development of the South Saskatchewan river to provide irrigation and an adequate water supply for Moose Jaw and Regina.
The discussion so far has been centred around irrigation, but it seems to me that the purpose of P.F.R.A. should be broader than that. Irrigation is only one method of land use. We need legislation and aid, so that all our land may be put to the best use. The other day I was reading a publication which stated that eastern Canada had lost 4,000,000 acres of land that was once arable. Soil erosion due to water and wind is a grave problem. The United States estimate that they have permanently lost 50,000,000 acres of land because the soil has been badly eroded. It is estimated that an additional 50,000,000 acres of land have been severely damaged.
I should like to see incorporated in the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act provisions for payments to farmers for certain agricultural practices. In the 'United States payments are made for contour cultivation, regrassing and certain other agricultural practices, and I believe it is time that similar payments were made in this country. There is danger of our losing more land through improper agricultural practices than we could gain under adequate irrigation developments.
I believe Mr. Thomson will be a good man for the job, but I am wondering if the job will be good enough for the man. On many occasions Mr. Thomson has advocated that more money be spent, so that the land in this great nation may be better used and made more productive.
The P.F.R.A. estimates are the same this year as last, but last year provision was made in another place for the possible expenditure of $5,000,000 on irrigation developments. That particular sum has been cut to $1,000,000 this year. There has been an increase this year

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
over last of approximately $700,000 which may be used on the St. Mary river dam project. So that if we compare the total provision for irrigation and P.F.R.A. this year and last year, there is some $3,300,000 less this year. It can easily be seen therefore that the government is not in earnest in trying to bring under irrigation land that it is feasible to irrigate. Instead the minister announces that it will take another two years.
I have here a report of the Saskatchewan reconstruction council in 1944, based on evidence given to the council by Mr. George Spence, who was then with the P.F.R.A. In their report they then came to the conclusion that certain projects are feasible. But now, four years later, this government is still in no position to tell the people of western Canada whether or not further irrigation projects will be undertaken.
