There has been a good deal of talk in the past of a bridge to be built over the South Saskatchewan river north of Swift Current. I think the federal government should be willing to provide some money for the building of this bridge, and not wish, as the minister stated, to leave it to the railways and provincial governments. The federal government provided for the settlement of people in that area of southern Saskatchewan. They have need of that bridge, and I think this government is responsible for providing money so that the bridge can be built.
The minister explained that he would have to take into consideration the provinces of Alberta and Manitoba in relation to the quantities of water that might be dammed in the province of Saskatchewan or in any other province. That certainly needs to be considered and a fair distribution should be made; but when the minister states that a dam cannot be undertaken until the reports are made, which will take at least two years, and that in the meantime the provinces must be got together, and that it will cost $66,000,000, for which no provision has been made and no guarantee can be given that the money will be spent, it seems to me that the government is not taking irrigation seriously at all.
This government can tackle any problem within the Dominion of Canada within its own jurisdiction and, I believe, can solve that problem within a reasonable period of time; and if it takes so much money over a period of two years to decide whether this particular dam or that particular project is feasible, I say that if the minister would spend twice as much money in one year he would probably arrive at the same result. The government should go ahead and spend the necessary money and provide irrigation instead of continuing to examine the feasibility one year after another, holding the carrot on the stick in front of the farmers of western Canada for a period of years and years.
Irrigation can increase the productivity of our soil tremendously. It has been estimated that up to 3,000,000 acres can be irrigated in western Canada. That amount of land would provide a good livelihood for thousands of farmers and increase the agricultural production of this country tremendously. It has often been said but it cannot be said too often that agriculture is our basic industry and that the prosperity of Canada depends on the prosperity of agriculture. Mr. Speaker, this prairie farm rehabilitation bill gives the minister power to appoint a director of rehabilitation, an associate director and other officers and employees and provides that the director and associate director may come within the pension provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act, with the approval of the treasury board. That was also done in another department with our ambassadors. They were given a pension and all that kind of thing. But I suppose these are "ambassadors of agriculture".
I cannot understand, as I travel about the country and look at our many idle Ontario farms why we cannot have a farm rehabilitation act applicable to Ontario. I believe in equality of treatment, and what is good for one province is good for another, following the old Cornish battle-cry, "Each for all and all for each". That is the principle underlying confederation. I see in Ontario, as I travel on the train, a great many farms which need rehabilitation, and they cannot get it.
The time has come when Ontario farmers should get some consideration, since this is concurrent jurisdiction, federal and provincial, because the consolidated revenue fund will be charged with this, and it will come out of the cash taxes of Canada. The two central provinces are paying over 72 per cent of the cash taxes. That is where the money will come from, and from the consolidated revenue fund. I am not objecting to the prairies getting everything they can, because I believe that they do need real assistance in this form and others. This is a protectionist doctrine of bonuses, subventions and subsidies, which the present minister, as a former free trader, opposed for many years. The government are now adopting all kinds of protectionist policies.
The time has come when there should be reciprocity in connection with rehabilitation of farms in this country. Dear knows in Ontario a great deal of rehabilitation is long over-due. It was held up because of the war and other conditions. I do hope that at the next session this act as to rehabilitation of farms will be made to apply to the industrial provinces and other parts of the country which need at once similar aid and help.

Mr. Speaker, before the house decides upon the principle of this bill by giving second reading to it, I wish to say a few words, which may not come within the exact terms of the bill
itself, but have to do with the principle involved. I think I have the right to do this on second reading.
The whole question of prairie farm rehabilitation is one which has been endorsed in principle in this house time after time for the very good reason that the work is necessary. Much of the work that has been done has been a great boon to western Canada. Coming from another part of the dominion, I also want to endorse the principle of prairie farm rehabilitation. I have never spoken on this subject before in the House of Commons, and I am not going to speak at any length this afternoon, but I want to point out one thing that logically follows what the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has just said.
I understand that in the eastern part of Canada we are to have an extension of the prairie farm rehabilitation principle. With that I am in entire agreement. Those of us who have seen the maritime marshlands and the need for some attention and government assistance will be of only one voice with respect to that proposal.
I want to point out to the minister and to the government that there is another problem facing many municipalities at the present time. Some of these municipalities are in my constituency, and because of that I have knowledge of it. In my part of the country it is not a question of where you are to find water, but what you are to do at times with the water that you have. The flood control problem this year has aroused the keenest kind of interest and concern in many parts of Ontario. I am not suggesting that it is not a matter of importance in other parts of Canada as well; but I want to point out to the minister, and particularly to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), who is in his place, and under whose jurisdiction this matter would normally come, that flood control is a serious matter in our province.
In Ontario in recent years legislation was passed dealing with the question of conservation. With the question of conservation is tied up the whole matter of flood control. In that legislation, which I am not going to place on Hansard because I am interested only in the principle of the thing, passed by the provincial government-a very advanced piece of legislation, which one would expect from a government in Ontario; by the way, it was unanimously supported by all parties in the legislature when it was introduced-provision was made that, in any area in Ontario where the question of flood control was an important one or the conservation of our natural resources was involved, the munici-

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act
palities which were closely connected with the area affected could set up what was known as a conservation authority.
The cost of such schemes of conservation and flood control was to be borne on a particular basis. The basis was this: 25 per cent to be put up by the municipalities involved, 37* per cent by the provincial government and 37J per cent by the dominion. The provincial government set as a condition of their putting up 371 per cent, and the municipalities as well, that they would be helped to the extent of 37^ per cent by the dominion government. In some instances, not many, these authorities have been set up. Certainly in the instance with respect to which I am going to speak, that of the Etobicoke conservation authority, it was properly set up.
Before the plan was finally put into operation, we had one of the most disastrous floods that have ever affected our part of the province in many years. I wish to point out that in my own town of Brampton the floods descended upon us in a way that we have never had before. The damage in the business section of that town of over 6,000 people amounted to over half a million dollars. Those of us who went to see the damage and the site after the flood realized that losses of that kind were beyond the capacity of an ordinary municipality to stand. Certainly in the case of that municipality the damage is so great that we shall be some time in getting over it.
To divert the Etobicoke river at that particular point would cost a considerable amount of money. Depending upon the plans which have been prepared by the department of planning and development of the provincial government, and which have been approved by them, I think, the cost would run more than $360,000 for one plan and nearly $750,000 for another to divert the Etobicoke river.
As soon as this matter came up, the difficulty we faced was that, while the provincial government was prepared to put up 37i per cent and the municipalities involved were prepared to give their share, the dominion government was not anxious to bear its share of the cost. The minister and I are too good friends for us to have a personal quarrel about a matter of this kind. He has been most courteous. His reception of the delegates who came here left nothing to be desired, but I wish to point out that from the standpoint of the policy of the government I think it is wrong. Before the government goes any further, it should announce a policy with respect to these control and conservation authority schemes and not allow the province of Ontario to have to bear the entire cost of the whole

75 per cent of the flood control scheme. If there ever was a reasonable case presented, and one that ought to have commended itself to the administration, this was one. I know the government takes this position: We are not interested in, nor have we any jurisdiction over, waters that are not navigable; why, therefore, should we have any part in this?
