1. Departmental administration, $234,297.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: Mr. Chairman, I have always been so much impressed with the importance of agriculture, that is, the growing of foodstuffs, that I am always concerned when I see the estimates of this department being reduced. When I find, by looking at the estimates for this year, that we have the sum of $13,000,000 of appropriations marked "not required for this year", it does seem a pity that that $13,000,000 could not be applied on various other items for the improvement of agriculture.
I wish to say, however, that I feel the minister has done an excellent job in his department. It is always interesting to me as an agriculturist to listen to what he has to say. I am not admitting that I am particularly enamoured of some of his policies, but when he has once made up his mind to pursue a certain path I think he does an excellent job and does what he believes to be the right thing.
I did not bring in any oleomargarine anyway.

Leave that to the
senators.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH: It should not be necessary in a country like this to emphasize the supreme importance of agriculture, but I feel that in Canada we treat the whole question too lightly and thoughtlessly. We have so much of the essential foodstuffs that we do not

Supply-Agriculture
give the matter very much thought. We take it for granted that we shall always have plenty, and I hope we always shall, but I should like to see every opportunity seized to lay before the members of this house and the people of this country the supreme importance of foodstuffs in this world.
The fact is that our potential population is outgrowing our potential production of foodstuffs. Agriculture is said to be the backbone of the country. As a rule, if the backbone of an organism is injured, the whole complex structure is in danger of deterioration. A careful reading of history discloses the fact that when the old civilizations were at their zenith, their agriculture, primitive though it was, was of the utmost importance and was both zealously guarded and encouraged. The realization was never lost sight of that disaster would be uncomfortably close if anything should happen to the growing of their foodstuffs and if their farmers were not completely protected both in the military and in the economic sense.
The value of foodstuffs was recognized as paramount in all these ancient civilizations; and, with the possible exception of Rome, the greatest care was exercised for many years to help their agriculture, to guard it against aggression by their warlike neighbours, and, what was equally important, to keep it economically stable and to give it that pride of performance without which no industry seems to be able to survive.
In every case, however, we find a gradual carelessness becoming apparent; a tendency to relegate agriculture or farming into a lower strata of human endeavour; to make of it a peasantry occupation; and it was at that point, we read, that the might of the nation began to wane. All these great and mighty empires long since have perished, and have been buried in the dust of humiliation and defeat. It is no coincidence that they followed their agriculture into oblivion. It is true that our own immediate situation is different, in that our own needs are in no great danger of being depleted to the point where we ourselves may have to go hungry; but unless we are willing to learn by the mistakes of others, we may find history repeating itself.
No nation seems to have been able to endure without a prosperous agriculture. For a short time it might, but eventually the position of agriculture in the economy of the nation appears to have established the stability of the economy itself.
I find that Doctor Walter Wilcox, of the University of Wisconsin, has called attention to the impact of world war II on pre-war food

production patterns of the world. He tells us that before the war, from 1935 to 1939, Asia, continental Europe and North Africa between them produced 68 per cent of the world's foodstuffs. North America is quoted as having produced 12 per cent of the world's food. That situation, of course, during and since the war has completely changed, and we find ourselves in the position of being responsible for a much greater percentage of the necessary food for the world in which we live. I was quoting history a few moments ago. An old Greek philosopher Xenophon who, incidentally, was not a farmer and not an agriculturist, but a philosopher and a general, a soldier, a disciple of Socrates, and who lived probably 400 years B.C., had this to say. I think the committee will find it interesting. Talking about farming, he said:
Yet tho it offers blessings in the greatest plenty, it does not permit us to take them in idleness, but requires us to accustom ourselves to endure the colds of winter and the heat of summer; to those whom it exercises in manual labour, it gives an increase of strength; and in such as only oversee the cultivation of it, it produces a manly vigour by requiring them to rise early in the morning and forcing them to move about with activity, for in the country as in the city, the most important matters are always done at a stated season.
I should be surprised for my own part if any man of liberal feelings has met with any possession more pleasing than a farm or discovered any pursuit more attractive, or more conducive to the means of life than agriculture.
The earth also kindly teaches men justice, at least such as are able to learn: for it is those who treat her best that she recompenses with the most numerous benefits.
He also said well, who pronounced agriculture to be the mother and nurse of other arts; for when agriculture flourishes, all other pursuits are in full vigour; but when the ground is forced to lie barren, other occupations are almost stopped, as -well by land as by sea. Agriculture is an art that renders those who understand it Tich, and leaves those who do not understand it, however much they labour ,in it, to live in poverty.
Since we have been allowed to live in a land which produces enormous quantities of foodstuffs, it does seem to me that we have a definite responsibility toward the rest of the world in growing as much as we can possibly grow and in as good quality as we can possibly secure. It is a duty as well as a responsibility, and I think an appeal should be made to the hearts of all the people who are concerned, and indeed to those people who are not closely concerned, to try to realize as a tremendous fact that, since we have the land and are able to grow this food, it is our business to do it to the best of our ability. If, however, it is not possible to appeal to the

Supply-Agriculture
hearts it might be possible to appeal to the heads, because, if I may quote Xenophon again:
When agriculture flourishes all other pursuits are in full vigour.
I wonder whether we have noticed that in this country. If we have noticed it, why have we not taken advantage of it? If we do admit that to be the fact, then surely there is something that we can do about it that we are not doing because, from my own experience of a good many years, agriculture has rarely been in a flourishing condition. I have also noted that when agriculture is not in a flourishing condition other industries of the country follow it along the same track.
I should also like to point out that if the farmers of our country have sufficient money to enable them to buy necessary things they will keep practically every industry in this country busy for a long, long time. There are so many things that they have not got, that they require, want and would be willing to buy, if they had the wherewithal, that they would keep industry going for a long time The other day the minister spoke about electric wind chargers. I venture to say that a very small percentage of Canadian farmers have electric wind chargers, but I also venture to say that they would all like to have one and undoubtedly would all buy one if they could get in the position where they had the money to spend on it. The same principle applies to other things. The home market, the guaranteed market, not the one we have to compete with other nations or other countries to hold or to secure, is there waiting for us if we could only do something for these people to put them into that position, to put them into w'hat Xenophon calls a flourishing position.
That there is a decline in our own agriculture is shown in the Livestock Market Review of April 29. In that review we find that the sows, which are the breeding stock of the hog industry, killed from January 1 to May 6, numbered 56,138. In that short period of time thousands and thousands of other young sows were also killed. These sows would be classed among our A's and B's in the hog classification, sows which could have been and probably would have been used as breeding stock if conditions were favourable for them to be so used.
From January 1 to April 30 the quantity of hogs had decreased from 1,836,618 to
1,335,000,	which represents a decrease of 27-4 per cent. Obviously something is slipping. I should also like to refer to the creamery butter output in my own province of Saskatchewan. This report is a year old. Probably the situation is even worse today. There was a decrease in the production of 1946 from 1945 of slightly more than 20 per cent.
I should like to talk about one other thing for a few minutes, namely the work of our scientists. When I first came to this country a good many years ago the limit of the wheat-growing land in Canada was very much farther south than it is at the present time. The farmer is said to be the last outpost of rugged individualism. I think that is the way it was put. I do not know of any other man who has depended so much upon the work of the scientist as has the farmer. When I first came to this country I could not grow wheat on my farm; it took too long. The old Red Fyfe wheat which was 'being used in those days had not sufficient time in that part of the country to mature. The scientists went to work and very soon had a variety which was much earlier, and now it can be grown not only on my own place but 100 miles north of where I live, which is a long way north. It means 100 miles north of Prince Albert. It is entirely as a result of the work of the scientists that this has come to pass.
I have glanced through a bulletin called "Scientific Agriculture," and I find in it a little item about a disease which is familiar to western men. Hon. members from the west will readily recognize it when I say I am referring to rust. I wonder if hon. members realize that in one year, 1916, the losses from rust amounted to 100,000,000 bushels in western Canada. The cash value of those losses in that year was $234 million.
I said that in 1916 we lost 100,000,000 bushels. In 1927 we lost 90,000,000 bushels and in 1935, over 87,000,000 bushels through this disease alone. I also pointed out that the value of the wheat in one year, 1916, was $234 million. The agricultural estimates for this year are $41,822,000. That is being set aside to take care of a loss that might happen again and might easily be $230 million. That does not seem very much to set aside. The loss in the year I have mentioned was almost six times the estimates of this year.
Other things are happening too. It is extraordinary that when we find a way to combat either a disease in plants or an insect pest or something of that kind, the plant disease or the insect pest finds a way of evading the cure. The bacteria find a way to outwit or to overcome the treatment imposed upon them, and it is an everlasting job. These
Supply-Agriculture

men must stay on the job all the time; their activities must never cease.
We had rust resistance long ago; nature provided it. We were never without rust resistant wheat, but the wheat that was rust resistant was no good for flour or bread, and again we had to go to the scientists to crossbreed a good quality variety with these rust-resistant varieties, which would provide us with something that would keep us in the wheat market so that we would not go absolutely broke when we tried to grow wheat.
There is trouble with other things besides grains. There are diseases in animals; it will take a long time for scientists to cure such diseases, and the fewer the scientists we have, the longer that time will be.
At this point I might be permitted to make a few comments on veterinary surgeons. When I was home at Easter I discovered in one part of the province a severe attack of Bang's disease and almost all the herds in that particular corner of the province had to be slaughtered. I have complained every year since coming here that the number of "vets" has been entirely too limited. More should be supplied or some method found to train more men for this particular service.
I am happy to say that in my own province the government has provided for scholarships to send men who are interested in veterinary work to the Ontario Agricultural College at Guelph where they specialize in this particular science.
I would ask the minister to consider doing something in the way of scholarships, or offering a remuneration of some kind, or some financial assistance to enable men, who cannot afford to pay their way, to attend these universities where they can pick up this particular science.
In conclusion, I should like to pay my respects to a man who has recently been superannuated from the central experimental farm, a man who has been responsible for a great deal of this plant work. I refer to Doctor Newman, dominion cerealist, who has been engaged in these activities for many years. I should like him to know that I, as a farmer and an old-timer in the west, appreciate the work he has done, and further, as an earnest of this appreciation which we should all show, I should like to see more funds allotted to take care of the training of men and the provision of research opportunities for our scientists.
I know that a good deal of money is spent on it, but I think it is insufficient. That applies not only to the resources at their disposal but also to the salaries which they 
receive. The loss of men is still going on and the principal reason is that they are going to better jobs, jobs which are better paid. Only in the last week one of the best men, in fact the only man they have ever had in the university at Saskatoon who has been making a special study into root systems, left the university, having gone to a job with an industrial firm. Now, as far as I know, that leaves the whole agricultural set-up without a man who has made studies in that direction.
These studies have been valuable, that being one angle of agriculture which no one ever thought of before, namely, exactly what a root system looked like and what it was responsible for. We knew that by putting in barley it smothered weeds; but why? We did not know except in a general way. It was sufficient for us to know that it did. We have found out that the principal reason for its doing so is the fact that it has a special root system. It has helped us because, knowing how the roots behave, we can govern ourselves accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, I had desired to devote some time to a discussion of the general topic which has occupied the hon. member who has taken his seat, namely the over-all importance of agriculture in the world in which we live. In the course of my discussion on that matter I was desirous of drawing the attention of hon. members to the possibility of rehabilitating some of the soils that have tended to become depleted and of preventing further depletion of our soils. May I direct the attention of the committee therefore, for a short time, to the question of the beet sugar industry as considered from that standpoint?
The beet sugar industry is an exceedingly important industry to Canada at the present time, far more important than it seems possible to get the average individual in the country to appreciate. It will ensure to Canada a sugar supply in peacetime and in wartime, and will ensure that supply at moderate prices. It will help to safeguard the economy against inflation. The beet sugar industry will stabilize agriculture as few industries in the country can. It will provide much employment for Canadians, and it will provide the cleaning cash crop that is essential to long-range successful irrigation projects, especially those on the prairies. The beet sugar industry will greatly augment Canada's real wealth and will conserve and improve Canadian soils.
May I discuss particularly this evening that aspect of the beet sugar industry in virtue of which it will conserve and improve Canadian soils. Before doing so, may I talk briefly regarding the general need in the world for

Supply-Agriculture
conserving soils and for rebuilding or rehabilitating the soils of the world. Until recently I had not had any kind of realization of how serious is the world's position with respect to its soils. May I pass on to the members of the house some of the considerations which have alarmed me to some extent. There is a rapidly growing shortage, as the previous speaker pointed out, of acres of land for the two billion-odd people in the world and that number of people is now rapidly increasing.
A book which will repay reading on the part of. any member of the house and any person in the country is one that has just been published by Mr. Fairfield Osborn. It is entitled "Our Plundered Planet." It was published in Toronto by McClelland and Stewart Limited in March, 1948. According to this writer, there are only about 16 billion acres of land in the world that could be thought of as originally favourable to the habitation of man. There are not more than four billion acres of arable land left, or less than two acres per capita. According to a United States department of state study, there were less than two and a half billion acres under cultivation before world war II. According to the best informed men, it takes two and a half acres of land of average productivity to support even a minimum adequate diet for each person in the world. Many countries have less than one acre per person.
These figures are sufficient to show how serious is the situation which confronts us as a world right now. The wastage of land has been and is alarming in Africa, as is developed in chapter VII of the book; in Australia and New Zealand, as is developed in chapter IX; in South America-which one eminent authority has characterized as being a "vanishing continent"-as is developed in one portion of the book; in Mexico and other world areas. These come near to home. I had not realized before I read it in this book that it takes between 300 and 1,P00 years for nature, under the best circumstances, to build one inch of topsoil. The one inch that we see carried away in a windstorm therefore represents nature's work of 1,000 years. Soil is not an easy thing to replace.
Proper agricultural methods, which are now well understood, are capable of preventing this destruction of soil. Until recently I had had the idea that science could play a much greater part in the production of foods for man than the writer of this book is inclined to think. He tells us that science cannot replace nature in providing food or in guaranteeing health. Both food and health can come only from a healthy soil. He discusses this matter in chapter V of his book under the heading, "The
Flattery of Science." May I quote from pages 75 and 76 of his book:
The issue might as well be clearly drawn. The- problem is how to conserve the remaining good natural soils that exist on the earth, together with the complementary resources of forests, water sources and the myriads of beneficial forms of animal life. There is no other problem. If that is not solved the threat to human life will grow in intensity and the present conditions of starvation that are already apparent in the various parts of the earth will seem as nothing in the years that lie ahead.
He closes his book with this solemn passage:
The tide of the earth's population is rising, the reservoir of the earth's living resources is falling. Technologists may outdo themselves in the creation of artificial substitutes for natural subsistence, and new areas, such as those in tropical or subtropical regions, may be adapted to human use, but even such recourses or developments cannot be expected to offset the present terrific attack upon the natural lifegiving elements of the earth.
There is only one solution. Man must recognize the necessity of co-operating with nature. He must temper his demands and use and conserve the natural living resources of this earth in a manner that alone can provide for the continuation of his civilization. The final answer is to be found only through comprehension of the enduring processes of nature. The time for defiance is at an end.
What is the general importance of all this to Canada? I believe every member of the house, after he examines these facts, will realize yet more that it is very serious. What have we done with our soils? All one needs to do is to look over the farms in Ontario in many parts, the farms in the maritime provinces in many parts, and the farms in certain western areas and to note the great number of them now deserted, in order to be impressed to some extent with what we have done.
What are we doing? I submit that, considering the wastage now going on in Canadian agricultural areas, what we are doing is meagre indeed. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who, more than any other minister who has ever had responsibility in Canada, has done much for the arresting of the decay or deterioration of the soil, will be the first to acknowledge that our efforts are far short of what is necessary to keep our soils from deteriorating further.
The question then is: What shall we do? That problem is not easy to answer in full. However I should like to make one or two observations which might be of some value in connection with the general answer to the problem. Are there crops which will rebuild the soil and at the same time pay returns? That is the question which would be asked first and foremost. And the answer must be that there are such crops.
Supply-Agriculture

One of these crops which will give very satisfactory returns, and at the same time rebuild the soil-in fact make it better than it ever was-is the sugar beet. May I for a time discuss the facts which will support the statement I have just made. Germany between 1870 and 1903 so improved her soils through sugar beet culture, and the crop rotation necessary in that culture, that she increased the production of her soils in respect even of cereals from 14 bushels to the acre, when she commenced the culture of sugar beets, to 34-9 bushels per acre at the end of the period I have indicated.
That was a genuine achievement. Over the period between 1879 and 1909 Germany became the greatest grower of sugar beets in the world. She increased her average yield of cereals by 80 per cent during that period. Over the five-year period of 1919 to 1923 Germany's average yield of wheat was 26 bushels per acre, while Canada's average during the same period was 16-04 bushels. Considering the fact that Germany is a very old; country, having been the scene of civilization in the long ago, while Canada is a brand new country, I believe those figures ought to bear considerable significance.
Here are some statements which have some weight in this connection. In a statement issued by a conference of continental experts on beet cultivation, convened by the economic committee of the league of nations, the French expert stated:
As beet growers we are concerned less with the production of sugar in itself than with the capital importance of the production of beet in our national economic lives.
Again in a report presented to the conference by Messrs. F. O. Licht, the well-known international sugar statisticians, it was observed that:
The reason why all governments cling so stubbornly to beet culture is not to be found mainly in consideration of financial policy but in agricultural and social considerations. Beet culture in itself, without reference to sugar production, is for many reasons a vital condition of all intensive agriculture.
During the period of 1870 to 1903 Germany subsidized her sugar beet industry to the extent of $340 million. May I for just a moment comment upon what, on the contrary, is being contemplated today in Canada. We have been told in the house by our selfassured Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that he will not support subsidies for the beet sugar industry. When we contrast his wisdom with the wisdom of the men whose words I have just read, we must wonder whether or not our brilliant young Minister of Finance has not been weighed in the balance and found wanting.

How does the beet sugar industry conserve and improve the soil to produce the results which I have indicated? There are several means. There is nothing mysterious about it; there is nothing accidental. The cultivation required in order to produce good crops of sugar beets pulverizes the soil, deepens the tilth and aerates the soil, and consequently warms it, thereby making a fine and congenial environment in which soil bacteria may thrive.
All hon. members are familiar with the importance of bacteria in the soil. Mr. Osborn points out that the bacteria are the things which make the soil living; and he implies, if not definitely states, that anything but a living soil is not a healthy soil.
The beet itself definitely improves the soil, physically and chemically. A healthy sugar beet sends out a mass of tap roots through six cubic feet of soil. The decomposition of these tap roots enriches the soil. It leaves tiny channels all through the soil, through which water and air may penetrate. When one remembers that on an acre of a good stand of sugar beets there will be between 16,000 and 26,000 individual roots or beets, and when he reflects that each of these 16,000 to 26,000 penetrates six cubic feet of earth he begins to have some understanding of and some means of computing the possible net effect on the soil of all the tap roots sent out into the soil by that number of beets. And of course when the beets are taken up all the roots are left in the soil.
An important element in successful beet culture is crop rotation, something with which every member of the house is thoroughly familiar. The crop rotation which is in use in the preparation of land for sugar beets includes legumes, usually either alfalfa or sweet clover. All hon. members know that on the roots of a legume are found little nodules. In those nodules live bacteria which have the power to take from the air free nitrogen and fix it in the form of nitrates, thereby rendering it available to plants for use in the production of proteins.
Therefore the legume which comes regularly in the rotation every three, five, seven or ten years, according to the particular kind of rotation employed, adds nitrogen to the soil through the nodules. A legume also adds fibre to the soil through the roots, long and tough, which are thrust deep into the soil in every direction. A legume aerates the soil, thereby encouraging bacterial growth.
The importance of bacteria in creating healthy soil and in nourishing a healthy crop may be indicated by the following facts. Bacteria change organic matter to ammonia;

Supply-Agriculture
other bacteria change. ammonia to nitrites while other bacteria change nitrites to nitrates. Consequently bacteria are responsible for the changing of organic materials such as manure and plant remains in the soil into forms available to plants. Consequently, if the soil is not congenial to the development of healthy growing bacteria it will be impossible for the soil to be thoroughly enriched by the application of manure. Bacteria pick up iron and render it available to the plant. Bacteria pick up phosphorus and render it available to plants. We realize, therefore, that there is a vast importance to be attached to bacteria in cultural preparations for crops. And so anything which stimulates the development of bacteria is of great value in the rebuilding, reconditioning and rehabilitating of the soil.
In all successful beet culture manure is spread. Manure constitutes a congenial environment for bacteria.
Almost all people who raise beets for sugar production carry on stock feeding as part of their operations, particularly the raising of beef and sheep. These two kinds of animals consume the beet tops which in southern Alberta, for example, are usually left on the ground and pastured by the stock from the ground after topping. It is quite obvious that if the stock are turned in on the beet tops and range over the field considerable fertilization results.
The tops from an average ton of beets will replace 150 pounds of alfalfa hay and 46 pounds of grain. The tops at the time of topping have a high feeding value for stock. Another by-product of sugar beet raising is beet pulp. A ton of siloed beet pulp is equivalent to 139-9 pounds of ground barley, 636 pounds of alfalfa hay and 44-2 pounds of beet molasses. Nearly every milk and butterfat producing record made in Europe and the United States has been made by cows fed beet pulp. The meat producing value of beet pulp is also very great. Then we have the beet molasses, which is the liquid that remains after all the sugar that can economically 'be taken from the beet juice has been extracted. In meat production the various by-products from an average acre of sugar beets, quite apart from the sugar produced, are equal in feeding value to that of the production of corn from an average acre.
In any good crop rotation used for the preparation of land for beets there will be, as I have indicated, alfalfa or a legume which produces a great deal of hay. There is always a great deal of straw produced when grain is raised upon land following beets.
Consequently in any beet producing area there will be an abundance of hay and straw. From what I have said it can readily be seen by all hon. members that the beet producing industry is conducive to the raising and supporting of livestock.
May I spend just a moment to emphasize the importance of animals in the development of soil. When our forefathers came to this country there ranged over the plains tens of millions of buffalo, scores of millions of deer, wild animals of the widest variety and vast flocks of game birds. Now the wild life is largely gone and with it have gone the good soil effects that came from it. In the days that we all can remember we used livestock for power on the farm and for transportation. We used horses and our forefathers used oxen. Those animals enriched the soil, but they have now been replaced through mechanization. This is going to have a bad result upon our soil. There must be something consciously done in the conduct of our agricultural practice to make up for the loss which we sustain through the displacement of animals; otherwise we shall have no healthy soil, because healthy soil depends upon animal life. Animals raised in connection with the beet sugar industry will help.
To what extent would Canadian soil benefit from the beet sugar industry? If we were producing all our sugar requirements from sugar beets we would be improving regularly every year at least one million acres of our soil. It takes about 15,000 acres of beets to produce one-twentieth of Canada's annual sugar requirements. To produce our total yearly needs would require 300,000 acres. The ordinary crop rotation employed in the preparing of soil for the production of beets averages four years, although some rotations run as long as ten years. This means that there would be in process of rebuilding and reconditioning incident to the production of sugar beets at least 1,000,000 acres of our soil. What effect that would have on the future of Canada over the period of a hundred years is a consideration which we should not lightly disregard. I recommend that thought to the minister's most careful attention.
We could have beet sugar for export. The proposal is thoroughly feasible. But there has been such a determined propaganda, cunningly and in many cases lyingly concocted, and deliberately distributed throughout this country to disparage beet production that people have never come to realize that Canada is one of the greatest potential sugar-producing areas in the world.
Supply-Agriculture
Can she compete with tropical countries?

I think so, with complete success. I shall deal with that aspect at some future time, as I do not wish to weary the house unduly now.
This matter of beet sugar culture and its importance, Mr. Chairman, is one which requires much study. It is impossible to deal with it all fully in one talk in this house. I say it is perfectly reasonable for Canada to contemplate the production of sugar for export. It is not generally known that Canada has been a considerable exporter of sugar in the years from 1916 to 1939. I have the figures here, which with the consent of the house I shall be glad to place on Hansard, but which I fear I shall not have time to read. They indicate that Canada has imported a great deal of cane, raw, refined it, and then exported it. That sugar might just as well have come from Canadian-produced1 sugar beets, going into the making of Canadian jams and other products.
The next question I may be asked is: Does the sugar beet thrive in Canada? The sugar beet thrives astonishingly well, especially in southern Alberta. I do not feel competent to speak for other areas, but I know what takes place in my own constituency. For example, I select one man, Ivan Harris, in the Taber area in my constituency. This man has produced 19-45 tons average per acre for eight years. That is a surprising yield. The sugar content in southern Alberta is extremely high. In the year 1939, for example, it was 17-688. There will hardly be an area on the American continent, except possibly California, where the sugar content would be so high. The extraction is always good. The production of beets is a thoroughly economic and profitable occupation.
What should we do to make sure that Canada will expand her beet sugar production? There are three things, Mr. Chairman, and I suggest to the minister most earnestly that he use his influence to the extreme to have these three things done right away this year. We are in danger of having one of our sugar factories in Ontario lie idle this year.
The main thing that should be done is to pay the beet sugar producers in Canada this year a price equal to the price which we are paying Santo Domingo cane producers for their cane sugar. Certainly it is the barest kind of justice to give your own producers the same price you are giving to foreign producers. That price would mean S8.64 per hundredweight at the refining centre.
I close by reading a statement from the submission of the beet producers in January, 1948,

to the Hon. D. C. Abbott, a submission which I fear has been completely disregarded by that exceedingly wise young man. Here are three of the recommendations:
1.	Guarantee the Canadian producer a fixed price for his 1948 crop made up as follows- Sugar (at San Domingo guaranteed price) $5 per hundred pounds, freight 40 cents per hundred pounds, duty $1.29 per hundred pounds and refiners spread $1.95 per hundred pounds, a total of $8.64 per hundred pounds at Canadian refining centres. This price to be adjusted at outside points to conform with the seasonal winter or summer freight rates.
2.	Restore the fixed valuation and at a price of $5.65 per hundred pounds.
4. Announce approval of the above at the earliest possible date.
Up to the present time, Mr. Chairman, not one of those things has been done. In other words, the treatment that Canada has accorded her beet sugar producers has been shabby. It has been unbecoming on the part of any intelligent government in any progressive country in the world today. May I urge that the minister take steps immediately to see that this situation is rectified so that the production of beet sugar in Canada will expand?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Lethbridge has spoken about the problems in his part of the country and he has shown some persistence in his advocacy of the improvement of the sugar beet industry. Good for him! But, sir, I want to say a few words about a problem that is most interesting to the farmers and the population of my part of the country, a problem with which the minister is thoroughly familiar, and that is the question of tuberculin tests in an area which has recently been established by the minister. For some time there has been a gap, and it still exists, between the counties of L'Islet and Rimouski. It was impossible for the farmers of the provincial counties of Riviere du Loup and Kamouraska to have tuberculin tests for their cattle. For many years we did not have any, and on that account it was impossible to buy stock from the farmers. Tuberculin tests are required by the farmers for their cattle and they are necessary also for the consumers of milk.
I had a lot of difficulty on account of the stupidity of an agronomist who has his office at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere and did not return all the petitions that were signed by the farmers of the three constituencies.
It is my duty to pay a special tribute to the provincial agronomists of the counties of Temiscouata and Riviere du Loup. They have taken a lot of trouble to try to secure an area for cheap tuberculin tests for the immunization of herds.

Supply-Agriculture
I had some correspondence with the minister, and he told me that a veterinary surgeon from my county would be appointed for our district, but at the same time there was a man in the department in Montreal who had assigned the very same doctor to the district of Rimouski. This was unsatisfactory, and I reviewed the case with the minister. He understood that there were many good reasons for granting my request. Now the area has been established, and I thank the minister for that. I ask him now when the tests will be made for the first time and be continued in Temiscouata county. I hope it will be soon.

May I reply to the last question? The matter was before me just this morning in a letter which was received in reply to a previous letter, and I have asked the officials to do everything possible to bring that area under inspection at an early day.
I thank the minister.

I should like to ask the hon. member for Temiscouata a question. I should like to know whether the farmers in his area are still being required to purchase flour at the present time when they purchase feed, as he complained they used to have to do a year or so ago.

Well, I cannot tell my hon. friend what is going on now, because I have not been in contact with them as I was before the session. When I go home for a day or two I do not inquire about it, but I know that the facts I have stated are perfectly true. I regret very much that I am not in a position to tell him what the situation is now, and I know very well that, as soon as the session is over, I will meet my people who will tell me if there has been some improvement. I shall tell the hon. member now something that may surprise him very much. It is that large numbers of the farmers of my county, instead of buying feed from La Co-operative Federee, are buying feed from grain merchants in Montreal and Quebec, and they are better satisfied in buying there than in buying anywhere else.

I think I should say something at this time about the dissatisfaction among the farmers with regard to marketing and some other matters. For some time farm organizations have been petitioning and asking the government to bring in a marketing act, to establish floor prices for agricultural products, prices that will have some relationship to and be on a parity with the things farmers have to buy.
We have heard a lot about wheat prices. Dollar wheat is just as good to me as $2 wheat if one dollar will buy as much as $2. It is not
the price; it is the things that wheat will buy. For a long time farm organizations have been asking for an agricultural marketing act with adequate farmer representation to market our farm products. If we had had that kind of act we would not have had the mess that we have been in this year in connection with coarse grains and hog prices.
I should like to read some letters which have been forwarded to me in connection with the hog business. I have a letter from a man who says, "I killed thirty-eight small pigs." Another says, "I killed a dozen pigs last fall as a result of higher grain prices." I have another letter which says, "I killed about thirty-four weaner pigs when the grain went up." I have a further letter which says:
I had twenty-five brood1 sows and hundreds of small pigs of different size. I killed over a hundred weaner pigs and new-born pigs and sold all my sows but eight. Most of those sold were heavy in pig.
Another letter says:
I did not kill any weaner pigs, when prices went up, but I did kill some when they were born and shipped sows that were ready to farrow.
It looks to me, Mr. Chairman, that in the coming year we shall not have enough pigs to supply pork for Canadians, to say nothing about exporting. These things seem to be pretty general in the part of the country from which I come and from the Alberta country around Edmonton where they have raised a lot of pigs. I believe the same thing is happening there. If we had a marketing board with farmers' representation on it, it would have been in touch with the government and would have taken a lot of responsibility off the government's hands. That would have been a very fine arrangement; but we were left absolutely in the dark in connection with all these matters. The same thing applies to wheat. There is great dissatisfaction among the farmers with respect to the sale of wheat over the past number of years, particularly domestically consumed wheat.
I calculated that we have sold 335 million bushels of wheat at thirty cents a bushel below the $1.55 export price. What farmers want to know is why they have to sell this wheat at thirty cents a bushel below the export price. I have been asked to find out why they were put in that position. No other business was put in that position. There was a ceiling price on domestically consumed wheat, although some time ago the Minister of Agriculture said there was never a ceiling price put on wheat. As I understand it, there was absolutely and definitely a ceiling price put on domestically consumed wheat,
Supply-Agriculture

because we receive no further payment on it. If a board had been set up with farm representation on it I am sure that we would not have suffered that loss.
I hold in my hand sessional paper 115A, dated February 4, 1948. This shows that in August, 1944, domestically consumed wheat sold at $125. There was a ceiling price of $1.25 to mutual aid countries till March, 1945. To non-mutual aid countries it ran from $1.35 to $1.52. From March, 1945, to January, 1946, the export price was $1.46 to $1.55 for mutual aid countries, but we were still supplying Canada with wheat at $125. In addition, Mr. Chairman, in December, 1947, class 2 wheat was selling on the world market at $3.29. It was only in February, 1947, that the price was raised from $1.25 to $1.55 on domestically consumed wheat. Can the minister explain why this amount of wheat that I have calculated at 335 million bushels was sold at that price?
I am very glad that the Minister of Agriculture is taking an interest in the dry parts of Saskatchewan from the standpoint of tillage. The hon. member for Lethbridge had something to say about beet growing and its advantages to the land. In our part of the country, carrying on dry farming, beet growing is entirely out of the picture. It is not practical in that part of the country where irrigation is not carried on. We have a strictly 50 per cent summer-fallow country which grows ten crops in twenty years. With the new method of tillage, using the combine and the one-way disc, I would say that we build up the soil instead of depleting it. If you have a crop of wheat it will take three pounds of twine to the acre to bind it. We do not get that every year. You only take the wheat; all the straw that is left, the chaff, you mix with the soil, and in the course of one year's summer-fallow and the following year, it is pretty well absorbed.
I should like to speak for a minute or so of a chemical weed killer that has been developed. It takes care of practically every weed we have in that part of the country. It saves stirring up of the soil. You have to work land to kill weeds and if the soil does not have the necessary amount of moisture and is worked when the land is dry, the bacteria are destroyed and dead land is left.
I am glad that the Department of Agriculture is experimenting in connection with the matter. The department has done a fine job so far in the experiments it has carried out. Would the minister care to give an explanation in regard to the ceiling price on domestic wheat?
That is not in my department.	-
It has to do with agriculture and I thought that perhaps the minister would like to say something about it.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take a few minutes to express the pleasure it gives me, the greatest pleasure since I have been a member of the house, in congratulating the Minister of Agriculture on two counts. First of all, I congratulate him because I know he is a thoroughbred Liberal, which is something in these days of reorientation in politics, and, second, I congratulate him on behalf of my constituents, the farmers of Matapedia, who have at last succeeded in receiving from the minister the assurance of a substation as an experimental farm in my riding.
As many members possibly know, in that part of the Gaspe peninsula, which region was the first to be discovered and the last to be reckoned with, it is a source of satisfaction to see at last a member of the cabinet and a good Liberal who is liberal enough, even if he does come from the west, to develop agriculture in that eastern remote area of the country.
The minister may rest assured that from everybody concerned he will receive the best wishes. He will remain in their hearts and minds longer than he may live, and let us hope that God gives him a long time yet in the service of the country.
I would also mention to the minister that the farmers of my riding have understood in these difficult times the problems that have arisen in connection with coarse grains. Of course they supported the policy of subsidies. They realize that the problem of whoever may be the minister in the House of Commons having to deal with nine other ministers of agriculture in Canada, is one of the most difficult so far as the relations between the provinces and the federal government are concerned. They also realize with the greatest pleasure that the minister has done the best he possibly can, to enable the farmers to carry on since the subsidies were taken off. He succeeded in having the freight paid on coarse grains coming from the west to the eastern provinces. Every one in my district appreciates immensely what has been done during this very session to help the farmers under the circumstances.
Once more I thank the minister for having given that station, which I am sure will help more than anything that has been done so far by the provincial legislature to promote agriculture by the best means, namely education.

Supply-A griculture
I have no doubt the station will do more for the farmers of that region than they have yet experienced.

A few days ago the Minister of Agriculture made reference to parsons who were not practising the profession in which they had been trained. I should like this evening to practise what I preach by returning good for evil and extending to the minister my best wishes when his party selects a leader this coming summer. If I were a Liberal I would consider the chances of electing a government as bright with the Minister of Agriculture leading the party as they would be with anyone else who appears on the horizon. However I wish to make it clearly understood that, should he be selected as leader and become Prime Minister, I shall do all I can to see that he does not retain the office for too long a period.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is indeed good for evil.

May I crave the indulgence of the house in order to raise a question which I do not think has been raised before in connection with agriculture? I refer to rural housing. I think I am in order, because the Minister of Agriculture has published two interesting studies, one in 1945, an "Economic Study of Land Settlement in Representative Pioneer Areas of Northern Saskatchewan", by R. A. Stutt and H. Van Vliet of the economic division, and the Economic Annalist of 1943, which contains an interesting section on rural housing. The department, under the experimental farms branch, has supplied quite a number of interesting plans for rural housing.
Unfortunately, in the estimates, we have not an item providing for any worthwhile assistance in dealing with this national problem, and therefore I should like to take a little time tonight to discuss the subject in the hope that in the next year the minister will find it possible to make provision for adequate subsidies to people in the rural parts of Canada who have the misfortune to live in houses that do not meet with modern standards in Canada and in other countries of the world, and who for a variety of reasons have not seen fit or have not been able to provide modern-type housing.
I commend to hon. members the study of Professor Van Vliet and Mr. Stutt who travelled extensively in Saskatchewan studying housing conditions in representative areas. Mr. Stutt expresses the opinion that improvements in the conditions of farm homes in
Saskatchewan are badly needed and that some thought should be given toward rural housing in a broad reconstruction program.
There were three representative areas taken: the prairie area, the park belt and the pioneer area in the north. In the well-established municipalities in the prairies around Wilcox, Wey-burn and Lacadena, it was found that 23-5 per cent of the farm houses were in poor condition. In the prairie belt, the area represented by the Minister of Agriculture, up around Melfort and Lashburn where the hon. member for North Battleford lives, 31-6 per cent of the houses were described to be in poor condition. Away up to the north, in the frontier areas, 56-5 per cent were in poor condition. According to this study, only six per cent of the farm houses in Saskatchewan were described to be in good condition. The farm houses in poor condition were valued at an average of $421 in the prairie district, $362 in the park belt and $202 in the pioneer district.
Those who are interested in the construction industry will agree readily that, with such a low investment in farm houses, we have a wonderful potential market for lumber, cement and plumbing supplies and potential employment for carpenters, plumbers and tinsmiths for many years to come.
While this study is confined to Saskatchewan, I understand that in Alberta and Manitoba similar conditions prevail. The 1941 census discloses that only 20 per cent of the farm homes in Canada had electric lights. The percentage in Ontario and in British Columbia is relatively high: it is 37 per cent in Ontario, 36 per cent in British Columbia, with 5-5 per cent in Prince Edward Island and Alberta and 4-8 per cent in Saskatchewan.
What is the percentage in New Brunswick?

I am sorry I have not that available. Unfortunately we in Saskatchewan are at the bottom of the list. I may mention that those statistics were for 1941, so that the C.C.F. government cannot receive any credit or blame for the conditions.
In all of Canada only 7-3 per cent of the farmers are able to use anything but the old washbasin or washtub on Saturday night for the traditional bath; only eight farmers out of 100 have flush toilets; and again the conditions in the prairie provinces are much worse. The conditions in the constituency represented by the Minister of Agriculture and myself are well below the average. In Mackenzie constituency only 2-4 per cent of the farmers have furnaces, whereas in Melville eleven per cent
Supply-Agriculture

have furnaces. In my constituency one farmer out of 1,000 lias running water in his house, compared with eleven out of 1,000 in Melville. Seventeen farmers out of 1,000 have electric light in my constituency, compared with thirty-eight out of 1,000 in Melville.
I know that in the pioneer days the people in Canada got along very well with candles and coal-oil lamps; but I am not one of those who subscribe to the theory that what was good enough for dad is good enough for me. We are now living in an age where there are unlimited electric slaves available to do our work. I think that the farm women in Canada should have first claim on these electric slaves to wash the clothes, to separate the cream and to do many of the jobs that are not being done by hired help. It was not so long ago that girls were available on farms for $5, $6 and 87 a month. They were not worried about the 40, 50, or 60-hour week. They worked from dawn until dark, seven days a week, and they did not expect holidays. But fortunately girls do not have to work for $5 a month nowadays; and farm women in every province are finding it difficult to get domestic help on the farm. Therefore, when the labour problem is so acute, it becomes a matter of national concern to have electricity made available on the farms.
I think members from every province have at one time or another said something about the migration from the country to the city. The Minister of Agriculture must take this into consideration and make some plans now to see if life on the farm cannot be made more attractive. The hon. member for Springfield will probably accuse me of running down my constituency, my province and the dominion. But I do not think you are running down your country when you face up to the facts and ask yourself the reasonable question: Can we not do something better? During the war I travelled up to the northern part of this dominion where we had large establishments of United States soldiers. It is difficult for me to explain to my people why they have to live in an area where only a few people can have electricity, running water and flush toilets; whereas when you go to Flin Flon, to The Pas or to Churchill, where long and severe winters are experienced, these facilities are available.
That is because they are in Manitoba.

Yes. But they did not have those conveniences at Churchill or Southampton island until the war. Up at

Flin Flon in Manitoba the people enjoy running water, telephones and modern conveniences.
The power is developed in Saskatchewan. We give it to them.

Yes, I was going to mention that. The power comes from Island Falls on the Churchill river. I am sorry that Island Falls is not built to accommodate tourists. But some day the life at Island Falls should be told to the people of the country. Possibly the people who work for the company there have the highest standard of living, on the average, that I have found anywhere in Canada. Every home has running water; every house is heated by electricity. All city conveniences are available up on the Churchill river in the far north. Therefore, if it is possible to provide those modern conveniences for those who supply electricity to produce minerals, the people who supply food to feed ourselves and the hungry people all over the world should have a return for what they produce so that they, too, can enjoy these modern conveniences.
This brings me now to a concrete proposal which I should like to make to the minister. It is that the next time his estimates come down he should make provision for subsidies for rural houses. I realize that he is in an awk-. ward position. Unfortunately the Secretary of State for External Affairs made a statement in Montreal last year which, in my opinion, will rule him out of the race for leadership. He was asked a question at the Liberal club at McGill; and as reported in the Montreal Gazette of October 8, in reply to the question:
How soon will subsidized housing make its appearance in Canada?
He said:
No government of which I am a part will pass such legislation.
He raised the old constitutional question that subsidized housing would be a threat to democracy and said:
Creating a bureaucratic body to allot such houses would be too easy a means for a vast Tammany Hall body and its ensuing corrup'-tion. . . We do not want to do favours for votes.
I think that was an unfortunate speech. I can realize that there is a difference of opinion in the cabinet regarding a matter of this kind. But I believe that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, if he had as much experience as the Minister of Agriculture has had, would have said that the government's policy will be announced in due course. And I

Supply-A gricul ture
am not surprised that the Minister of Agriculture is not able to get up now and announce that his department is prepared to provide subsidies to encourage farmers to improve their living quarters.
I would mention to the committee that we have a tradition or a precedent here. We have had before us today a measure respecting the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and it is significant that from no section of the house was there any criticism of this legislation. As a matter of fact, it is the most popular agricultural legislation that has been introduced, so far as western Canada is concerned, for many years.
I would point out that 33,823 farmers in the prairie provinces have been subsidized to the extent of $100 each. What for? To dig a dug-out on a farm. It could be argued that the government has no business giving a man money to improve his own property. But if the government had not provided these subsidies, Canada simply could not have filled her commitments in supplying food to a hungry world during the war. It would not have been possible during those years for the farmers to haul water four or five or six miles for their hogs and cattle. I submit that the subsidizing of 33,823 farmers to the tune of an average of $100 each was an excellent investment. And I am sure the Minister of Agriculture has won many friends by it.
It can be argued that legislation of this kind enables a minister to reward some of his friends by making them inspectors. But no one would ever accuse the Minister of Agriculture of doing anything of that sort. And whether or not one can reward his friends by making them inspectors, I do not recall a single member of any party ever saying, during a discussion of the estimates, that one cannot get a dug-out unless he is a Liberal.

If you are a Liberal
you need one.

I know there have been inspectors appointed who have probably made mistakes; but there are certainly a great many C.C.F. people in my constituency who have dug-outs and, so far as I know, there are not any whose applications for dug-outs have been turned down for political reasons. I believe I must say that in fairness to the minister. There might be the odd case, but I do not know of any; and usually such complaints are brought to the attention of members of parliament. Perhaps I shall get some letters from people whose applications have been refused. However, by and large, the inspectors go out and, if they strike a place where it is sandy,
they will decide that it would not be fair to use public funds in a place where a dug-out would not hold water. It would be of no use to the applicant or to the country.
So I am simply asking the Minister of Agriculture to go a step further in what will be an even more popular field, in deciding that something will be done to improve the housing on Canadian farms. The Curtis report emphasizes the fact that a major program will be required to bring up the housing standard of the farming population to a reasonable level. They divided our farmers into two groups, those who will be able to build new houses of their own, and farmers whose incomes are insufficient for them to undertake to build, without some measure of assistance.
We have had housing legislation in Canada since 1935, but it was not until three years ago that the rural housing section of the National Housing Act was declared. Thus far not a single farm house has been built in this country under the National Housing Act.
So I am suggesting that, if the minister wishes to get action, he should make provision in his department, as has been done in the United States, for a special housing branch to make plans and to provide subsidies.
The report also recommended that more work should be done in the field of design. The experimental farm service has, in connection with it, an architects branch. Unfortunately this branch is under-staffed and overworked; and it is necessary for it to prepare plans for buildings on the various experimental farms across Canada. Thus far they have not been able to design as many types of farm houses as might be desired.
When one considers the wide range of climatic conditions in Canada he must realize that we should have a staff working to prepare plans which would be of use, for instance, in Prince Edward Island, where they want to store large quantities of potatoes in the basement. And those of us who wish to build houses in northern Saskatchewan, where 40 degrees below zero weather is not unusual, will have to have other plans and other types of houses, while the fruit growers of British Columbia would require to build quite a different type.
The Curtis report suggests that a great deal more work should be done in the designing and planning of rural houses.
It also proposes that at least 100,000 farm houses should be accepted as a reasonable target to replace the obsolete and run-down farm houses. This would be only about fourteen per cent of the total number of farm dwell-
Supply-Agriculture

mgs, and just a little over a third of all the dwellings recorded in the last census as being in need of external repair.
To finance rural housing, this suggestion is made and if the minister acts along this line he will not be accused of adopting the C.C.F. policy; he will merely be following out the proposal made by a responsible committee appointed by his own government. The Curtis report suggests that a subsidy would be necessary either on a capital or on an interest basis. It was proposed that, instead of payments being calculated on a monthly basis, they should be related to the crop seasons with annual or semi-annual payments. I might mention again that this formula has been worked out satisfactorily in the United States.
The Curtis report also says that consideration should be given to granting physical needs such as electrical appliances, plumbing, heating and refrigeration equipment.
Then there is a whole section on farm housing of farm labourers. The Curtis report quite correctly points out that there is a problem in keeping farm help on our farms, and that many of the farmers have not additional rooms in their houses, with the result that the hired man must go to the attic or to the bam loft for his sleeping quarters. I have worked as a farm labourer, and I can say I would rather work as a farm labourer and live with the farmer than be a low-paid worker living in a slum area of a city. But if something could be done with a view to providing houses for farm help, many who are unable to buy farms of their own might look forward to marrying and settling down and enjoying life in rural communities.
So I suggest that something should be done with respect to giving further study to this problem. In asking that direct subsidies for housing in rural Canada be given, I am not suggesting something which has not been done. The government provided a production bonus of $400,000 to Crane Limited to induce them to turn out bathtubs last year. I submit that, politically and economically it would have been much better to spend $400,000 to help farmers in Canada to secure bathtubs. They should have some encouragement to purchase these commodities.
I do not deny that farm income at the present time is at a higher level than it has been for some time, and that more farmers are paying income tax than ever before. But the only times during my lifetime when the farmers had anything like a fair share of the national income were during world wTar I and world war II. Before world war I and in between the two wars, farmers in all parts

of Canada saw what happened to farm prices. As a result, many farmers who could now modernize their homes are building in the towns and cities. They realize that farm prices may go to pieces and that if they have their living quarters in a town or city they will be in a better position to get through the depression than if they continue to live on the farm.
How is the farmer going to live in town?
A great many in our province are operating farms five, eight or ten miles away.
But you said if there was a depression.

If there is a depression they will take a chance of getting relief in town. They would have a roof over their head and they know that during the hungry thirties people on relief in the town were able to get better medical care and had a higher standard of living than the people in the country. Some of them have profited by past experience and are going to take a chance on living in the town in the event of a depression.
Coming back to the subsidizing of Crane Limited, I submit that it is not in the public interest to spend $400,000 of the taxpayers' money to turn out bathtubs without asking some questions as to where those bathtubs are to be used. A hotel at Ste. Marguerite was burned this winter. It was a new hotel costing about $600,000, and in it were a large number of bathtubs made by Crane, I suppose, which had been subsidized by the Canadian people. Is it good policy to subsidize bathtubs for a luxury hotel when only seven farmers out of one hundred in Canada are able to have a bathtub for their Saturday night bath?
What kind of training were they doing in those bathtubs?

If the hon. member for Calgary East is no more interested in the housing problem than he appears to be, it is too bad for him.
To come back to this subsidy of $400,000, if it was government policy to see that more bathtubs were produced the same result could have been achieved by offering a subsidy to the farmer. You could grant a subsidy to every farmer who installed1 a bathtub in his home. That would be one way of guaranteeing production and of guaranteeing a market. So I submit that the minister should give consideration to doing for the farm population what the minister of reconstruction has been

Supply-Agriculture
doing for the people who live in high-priced hotels in tourist resorts in the mountains of Quebec and all across the country.
We had some experience in subsidized housing in Canada during the thirties. The federal, provincial andi municipal1 authorities subsidized houses for people in the cities who were unfortunate enough to be on relief, but it was a pretty pitiful performance. I have mentioned before the $50 which was paid to build a house of logs in the north country. There were a great many of them built. When the Liberal government took over, the subsidy was raised: to $75. During that period I travelled down to Montana, to Fort Peck, to see what President Roosevelt was doing as part of his resettlement program under the new deal. A huge dam was built, and along the Milk river farmers were re-established on small holdings where they were able to take advantage of the irrigation. They were able to live in modern bungalows with hardwood floors, furnaces, electric lights and running water, houses which cost a great deal more than $50.
I submit that, as part of a national policy, it was much better to build modern $4,000 houses which would give some comfort and satisfaction to people than to build $50 and $75 houses. It would have been quite simple for the federal government in those thirties to decide that no one should have to live in a $50 house, that we should not deny our people the right to have lumber for partitions when one could have lumber cut for $5 per thousand. A great many of these settlers were unable to get the $5 with which to cut their lumber. I saw settlers in the northern areas cutting lumber right out of the log with whipsaws. It was a costly process in terms of hours, but for people living on $8 or $9 a month it was the only way they could get lumber with which to build a school. I submit that we should profit by the experience of the United States where they provided houses during the depression that are still a pride to the people.
When the Labour government took over in New Zealand in 1935 they had as one of their main objectives the providing of decent housing for people on the farms, but probably one of the most outstanding examples in all the world in the field of rural housing is Sweden. Back in 1904, more than forty years ago, Sweden decided that it would be part of their public policy to encourage people to live on the farm. This policy was introduced when a great many people were leaving Sweden to come to the United States and Canada, while others were moving to the cities. A great many of them came here and became good citizens of this country.
The policy introduced in Sweden in 1904 has been well received. By 1945, 80,000 low-rental units had been built, of which 48,000, or well over 50 per cent, were agricultural holdings. In 1923 legislation was passed in Sweden to bonus home ownership improvements to a maximum amount of 1,500 kroner, or approximately $360. To qualify for the grant, an owner had to complete improvements to at least double the amount of the bonus. This is the same policy the minister carries out. He does not go on to a prairie farmer's farm and pay the entire cost of a dug-out. He says to the farmer, "If you pay part the government will pay part." In Sweden they say, "You spend at least $360 in improving your farm buildings and the government will spend $360."
Since 1933 loans have been available on favourable terms to provide workers in lumbering, agriculture and road making with a dwelling and a little land in order to make life somewhat easier when they are out of work. The amount which a borrower may obtain was fixed >at first at about $1,430; but since 1930, as a result of building costs, the maximum has been increased to $1,670. These amounts are not very high when one takes into account present-day costs, but I am speaking of conditions in Sweden in 1938 where building costs have always been a great deal lower than here.
The loans are free of interest and are nonredeemable during the first five years. At the end of this period, two-thirds of the capital sum are repayable by annual instalments of one-thirtieth. No interest is paid for thirty-five years and then only on the unredeemed balance of the capital.
In 1935 the Riksdag voted special credits to be allocated in the form of mortgage loans to farmers wishing to build or to adapt dwellings for their workers. The aim was to encourage the erection or reconditioning of farm workers' dwellings of a good type and suitable for their purpose from a social and hygienic point of view. There is no means test in connection with these applications. We do not have a means test on the prairies in connection with dug-outs.
The loans on farm workers' dwellings amount to not more than $715 for each separate dwelling and may not exceed 80 per cent of the estimated cost of the whole building. Originally it was provided that the loan was subject to 3-6 per cent interest, and amortization is at the rate of one-twentieth annually. In 1939 the Riksdag voted that these loans should be free of interest for the first half of the 20-year period of redemption.

Mr. Chairman, I have a matter to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture which created, a good deal of interest to those of us who live at the lake-head. When our exhibition was in full swing and everybody seemed to be enjoying it, a

team of horses that was hitched to a heavy truck became frightened and bolted, and they were heading for a group of men, women and children, many of whom no doubt would have been injured had not a young lady, Miss Ruth Black, who was distinguished for her horsemanship, jumped out and, after a tussle, grabbed the lines and in a short time brought the team under control. She received loud cheers from the spectators and got headlines in the local newspapers and was honoured locally. She is a daughter of our local veterinary surgeon and distinguished for her ladylike athletic endeavours, a girl who stands out permanently in the life of our city.
When a soldier distinguishes himself beyond his comrades we know that he receives honours and deserves them well. We are proud of our Victoria Cross men in this house. In peacetime when a man distinguishes himself by running great risks to save life we honour him. Much more should we honour a girl who so distinguished herself, and, at the risk of being knocked down and trampled by a team of horses, saves the lives of many women and children as this girl did. I think the Minister of Agriculture should honour this girl in a fitting way and I would ask him if he has any suggestion to make in this respect.
